studyMetadata.description: Are you growing in Christ? God wants all his children to grow in Jesus. If you are not growing, these studies will help you work out what is wrong and how to put it right. If you are growing, they will help you grow more. Working through Scripture, each session combines close reading with personal reflection. Volume 2 looks at shame, the gospel, idols and wisdom.

elements.text: ‘Guilt says you have done wrong; shame says you are wrong.’ Anon.

elements.question: What do you think of this quotation? Do you like it or not, and why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts…

elements.text: Have you ever felt so ashamed about something that you never wanted anyone to know? Luka felt like that. His story is true, and he has agreed to my telling it. I have changed his name. He had secretly struggled with pornography since his early teens. He had never spoken to anyone, and felt he never could. He had tried to stop, and sometimes managed it for a week or two, but he always fell back into the trap. No matter how hard he tried, or how much he fasted and prayed, the problem would not go away. He needed help, but he was too ashamed to ask for it.

elements.question: What would you tell Luka? What advice would you give him?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts…

elements.text: There are two problems in giving Luka advice. The easier problem is what to say. The harder problem is that you would not even know to say anything, because he is too ashamed to ask. You may know what this feels like from the inside, from the past or even now. Shame holds us back, but it can be overcome.

elements.question: Tap to see how guilt and shame differ.
elements.answer:
Guilt says, ‘I did something wrong.’ Shame says, ‘I am wrong.’

Shame is more than regret for an act. It is a painful sense that you yourself are unacceptable, whether because of what you did, what was done to you, or the people and things you are linked with.

elements.text: Made for honour
Humans were designed for honour, but sin twists that out of shape. Sin brings us dishonour, and it deceives us into seeking honour in the wrong places.

elements.passageText: 25The man and his wife were both naked, but they were not ashamed.

elements.question: What glimpse do we get here of how life without shame might have been?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at how the man and his wife felt about being seen by each other.
elements.sampleAnswer: The man and his wife were both naked, but they were not ashamed. There was nothing to hide: they could be fully known by each other, and by God, without embarrassment or fear. This is a glimpse of how God made life to be, with honour and without shame. It shows that shame was not part of God’s original design.

elements.passageText:
1Now the serpent was shrewder than any of the wild animals that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Is it really true that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the orchard’?” 2The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit from the trees of the orchard; 3but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the orchard God said, ‘You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or else you will die.’” 4The serpent said to the woman, “Surely you will not die, 5for God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will open and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

6When the woman saw that the tree produced fruit that was good for food, was attractive to the eye, and was desirable for making one wise, she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some of it to her husband who was with her, and he ate it. 7Then the eyes of both of them opened, and they knew they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.

8Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God moving about in the orchard at the breezy time of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the orchard. 9But the Lord God called to the man and said to him, “Where are you?” 10The man replied, “I heard you moving about in the orchard, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” 11And the Lord God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Did you eat from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” 12The man said, “The woman whom you gave me, she gave me some fruit from the tree and I ate it.” 13So the Lord God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” And the woman replied, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”

elements.question: In what ways does sin bring shame? What changes for Adam and Eve once they have eaten?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at verses 7 and 10 for what they now notice and feel.
elements.sampleAnswer: Once they have eaten, the eyes of both of them are opened and they know they are naked. The easy openness of Genesis 2:25 has gone and they feel exposed. When they hear the Lord God in the orchard, they are afraid and hide. Sin has brought shame, fear and distance from God and from each other.

elements.question: How do Adam and Eve try to escape from their shame?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice what they do in verses 7, 8, 12 and 13.
elements.sampleAnswer: They sew fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves. When they hear the Lord God, they hide among the trees. When God questions them, the man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent. Covering up, hiding and blaming others are all ways of trying to escape shame, and none of them works.

elements.text: After the Fall, we easily feel shame, and we do not like it. Like Adam and Eve, we look for ‘fig leaves’ to cover it, but fig leaves are full of gaps and make poor coverings. So we try to distract from our own shame by shaming or lowering someone else. That goes against what Jesus wants for us. Sin dishonours God, shames us before him and leaves us feeling ashamed, and the shame then pushes us into more sin.
The younger son

The younger son in Luke 15 brings shame upon his family. Asking for his inheritance is shameful. Wasting his money in the foreign land is shameful. When it runs out, he ends up in a shameful condition: penniless, tending unclean animals, and longing to eat their food. But to go back home and beg for mercy is also shameful, perhaps even more so. His shame is ‘shallow’ in the distant land because it happens among strangers. If he returns home, it will be ‘deep’: he will be shamed before his family, his friends and everyone who has known him from childhood.

elements.passageText: 18I will get up and go to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired workers.”’ 20So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way from home his father saw him, and his heart went out to him; he ran and hugged his son and kissed him. 21Then his son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22But the father said to his slaves, ‘Hurry! Bring the best robe, and put it on him! Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet! 23Bring the fattened calf and kill it! Let us eat and celebrate, 24because this son of mine was dead, and is alive again—he was lost and is found!’ So they began to celebrate.

elements.question: How does the younger son respond to his shameful situation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what he decides to say and admit in verses 18–19.
elements.sampleAnswer: He decides to get up and go to his father, and to say that he has sinned against heaven and against his father. He admits that he is no longer worthy to be called his son. He asks only to be treated like one of his father’s hired workers. He stops pretending and humbles himself, knowing there is nothing he can do to put things right.
keyTerms: get up|go to his father|went to his father

elements.text: You cannot lift yourself out of shame. Someone honourable has to reach down and lift you up.

elements.question: How does the father do this?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice what the father does before his son can finish his speech, and what he gives him.
elements.sampleAnswer: The father sees his son while he is still a long way off, and his heart goes out to him. He runs to him, hugs him and kisses him before the son can finish what he planned to say. Then he has the best robe, a ring and sandals put on him, and he calls for a feast. The father does not stand on his own honour; he reaches down into his son’s shame and lifts him out.

elements.text: The father is a picture of God’s grace to us in Christ, and of the same grace Jesus wants us to show one another. Grace feels like a gamble, because the father cannot make either son accept it. To follow Jesus often means going against the ‘proper’ ways of behaving that our world teaches us. Our world is more like the older brother.
The older brother

elements.passageText: 28But the older son became angry and refused to go in. His father came out and appealed to him, 29but he answered his father, ‘Look! These many years I have worked like a slave for you, and I never disobeyed your commands. Yet you never gave me even a goat so that I could celebrate with my friends! 30But when this son of yours came back, who has devoured your assets with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’

elements.question: (1) How does the older brother respond to his father’s celebration? (2) How, in his anger, does he fail to honour his father?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what he refuses to do, and at how he speaks to his father.
elements.sampleAnswer: The older brother is angry and refuses to go in to the celebration. He answers his father sharply: he says he has worked like a slave for him and never disobeyed, and complains that he was never given even a goat. He calls his brother ‘this son of yours’ instead of ‘my brother’. In his anger he dishonours his father by refusing to join the party, and does not notice it.

elements.text:
The older brother understands the ‘normal’ rules of honour and shame. His brother has acted shamefully, so he has lost his honour. He must live with his shame; indeed he ought to. In the older son’s eyes, the father is short-circuiting the world’s ‘natural justice’.

We are not told how the older son finally responds to his father’s grace. That leaves us to choose for ourselves:

  • Will we follow the world’s code of shaming the shameful and honouring the outwardly honourable, or will we agree with God’s radical reversal?
  • Will we openly acknowledge our own shame, whether hidden or not, humble ourselves before God, and let him welcome us?
Breaking the cycle

elements.passageText:
38“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ 39But I say to you, do not resist the evildoer. But whoever strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well. 40And if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your coat also. 41And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two. 42Give to the one who asks you, and do not reject the one who wants to borrow from you.

43“You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘hate your enemy.’ 44But I say to you, love your enemy and pray for those who persecute you, 45so that you may be like your Father in heaven, since he causes the sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. 46For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Even the tax collectors do the same, don’t they? 47And if you only greet your brothers, what more do you do? Even the Gentiles do the same, don’t they? 48So then, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

elements.question: What does Jesus tell us to do when someone wrongs or insults us (verses 38–42)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at the four examples: a slap, a lawsuit, forced service and a request.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says we are not to resist the evildoer by paying back like for like. If someone strikes us on the right cheek, we turn the other; if someone sues for our tunic, we give our coat as well; if someone forces us to go one mile, we go two; and we give to those who ask. This breaks the cycle of revenge and shame that the ‘eye for an eye’ rule keeps going. It is the opposite of the world’s code of honour.

elements.question: Whom does Jesus tell us to love, and what reason does he give (verses 43–48)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what the Father does for both the righteous and the unrighteous.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells us to love our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us. The reason is that this is what our Father in heaven is like: he causes the sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. Loving only those who love us is no better than what tax collectors and Gentiles do. We are to be perfect, as our heavenly Father is perfect.
keyTerms: tax collectors|love those who love you

elements.text:
God’s way of dealing with honour and shame is almost the exact opposite of the world’s way: the first will be last, and the last will be first; God lifts up the lowly, but brings down the proud.

  • In human culture: showing humility, putting others first and serving others means being shamed. Showing pride, putting yourself first and being served means being honoured.
  • In God’s Kingdom: it is the other way round. The humble who serve are honoured, and the proud who want to be served are shamed.

If your sense of who you are is not built securely on the fact that you are precious to God and loved by him, and if you are not confident that you are honoured by him, then, like the older son, you will look for honour and security through worldly shortcuts. Those shortcuts are at other people’s expense: you build yourself up by pulling others down.

elements.text:
In the next study we look at how God sees us, and at the way out of shame.

One note before you go. Not all shame comes from our own sin. If someone has abused you or wronged you, the shame you feel is not yours to carry, and you do not need to confess it as sin. Tell a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust.
‘Shame is basically the fear of being unlovable.’ Brené Brown

elements.text: To deal rightly with shame, we need to know how God himself sees us.
God and his children

elements.passageText:
17The Lord your God is in your midst;
he is a warrior who can deliver.
He takes great delight in you;
he renews you by his love;
he shouts for joy over you.”

elements.question: How does God feel about us, his children?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what the verse says God does, and how he feels, over his people.
elements.sampleAnswer: God is in the midst of his people, and he is a warrior who can deliver them. He takes great delight in them, renews them by his love and shouts for joy over them. This is not a God who is ashamed of his children or disappointed in them. He is strong enough to save us and tender enough to rejoice over us.

elements.passageText: 3Instead of being motivated by selfish ambition or vanity, each of you should, in humility, be moved to treat one another as more important than yourself. 4Each of you should be concerned not only about your own interests, but about the interests of others as well. 5You should have the same attitude toward one another that Christ Jesus had,

elements.question: How should we feel about others, and whose example do we follow?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice what we are to avoid, and whose attitude we are to share.
elements.sampleAnswer: We are not to act out of selfish ambition or vanity. In humility we are to treat one another as more important than ourselves, and to be concerned for others’ interests as well as our own. The example we follow is Christ Jesus, who had this attitude. This is the opposite of competing to look better than other people, which is how shame spreads in a community.

elements.text:
Our world builds communities on competition, and sometimes churches do so too. We create artificial versions of ourselves, ‘photoshopped’ to look as glorious as possible, and we hide our true selves behind the mask. We swap true community, where our true selves know one another and are known, for an artificial ‘masked community’.

Being confident in God’s love gives you the confidence to know that you cannot win your own honour. You have lost your honour through your sin, and yet you are honoured anyway. God has chosen you to be his child and adopted you into his family. You are a co-heir with Christ, and precious to the Almighty God of the universe. If you are confident in his love, you can be confident in this. If you forget his love, you may forget how honoured you are in him, and start looking for substitutes in all the wrong places.
Gaining confidence that our honour is found in God

Read the five verses below one at a time. For each one:

  • Meditate on it for at least 30 seconds, or longer if you can.
  • Ask yourself whether you ‘own’ the truth it expresses. Has it shaped your thinking?
  • Pray briefly, asking God to help you ‘own’ it, or to go on ‘owning’ it.

Psalm 62:7

elements.question: Jot down something you want to remember from each of these five verses.
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Take each verse in turn and note what it says about where your honour comes from.
elements.sampleAnswer: Psalm 62:7 says God delivers me and exalts me, and is my strong protector. 1 Samuel 2:8 says he lifts the weak and the poor and gives them an honoured position. Isaiah 54:4 promises that we will not be put to shame or humiliated. Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross, disregarding its shame, and now sits at God’s right hand. Romans 10:11 says that everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.

elements.text:
Can shame be positive, by discouraging us from doing wrong, so that we will not feel ashamed afterwards? Perhaps, in advance. But it changes after the sin has happened. The right response to sin is confession, repentance and forgiveness: to humble yourself, as the prodigal son did, and receive God’s grace. He lifts up the lowly.

The world’s view is that the lowly should be kept low. The best outcome may well be to avoid doing wrong. But if you have already done wrong, the world’s next best option is to cover it up and perhaps blame someone else. The worst option is to confess, because if you confess you lose face, lose status and lose honour.

  • In human culture: if you deny your sin, cover it up and blame someone else, you keep acceptance, status and honour. If you confess, you meet rejection, blame and shame.
  • In God’s Kingdom: if you confess your sin, repent and seek forgiveness, you receive acceptance, forgiveness and honour. If you deny and cover up, you meet rejection, blame and shame.

When you have done wrong, you cannot impress both the world and God.

elements.passageText:
2Many of those who sleep
in the dusty ground will awake—
some to everlasting life,
and others to shame and everlasting abhorrence.

elements.question: What does this verse say about the final verdict on people, and why does that make God’s view matter more than the world’s?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice the two different outcomes the verse describes, and how long they last.
elements.sampleAnswer: Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting abhorrence. The verse shows that there is a final verdict, and that both outcomes last for ever. The world’s honour and shame will not last, but God’s verdict does. So the choice of whose approval to live for matters far more than it seems at the time.

elements.passageText:
3When I refused to confess my sin,
my whole body wasted away,
while I groaned in pain all day long.
4For day and night you tormented me;
you tried to destroy me in the intense heat of summer. (Selah)
5Then I confessed my sin;
I no longer covered up my wrongdoing.
I said, “I will confess my rebellious acts to the Lord.”
And then you forgave my sins. (Selah)

elements.question: For someone who is trapped in shame, what is the way out?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare what happens while the writer keeps silent with what happens when he confesses.
elements.sampleAnswer: While the writer refused to confess, his body wasted away and he groaned in pain, for God’s hand was heavy on him day and night. The way out came when he confessed his sin and no longer covered up his wrongdoing. He said he would confess his rebellious acts to the Lord, and God forgave his sins. The way out of shame is to stop hiding and to bring it into the open before God.

elements.passageText: 16So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great effectiveness.

elements.question: What other advice does God’s word give us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at who we confess to, and what is promised.
elements.sampleAnswer: We are told to confess our sins to one another and to pray for one another. The purpose is that we may be healed. It is not enough to confess in private to God alone; God’s word expects us to share our struggles with other believers. The verse also says that the prayer of a righteous person has great effectiveness.

elements.passageText: 2Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

elements.question: Instead of carrying our shame and burdens alone, what should we do?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what we are to do with one another’s burdens, and what that fulfils.
elements.sampleAnswer: We should carry one another’s burdens. God does not expect us to carry the weight of sin and shame by ourselves. When we help bear each other’s burdens, we fulfil the law of Christ. That means being willing both to share our own burdens and to receive other people’s.

elements.text:
Choose the right person to talk to. The prodigal son confessed to his father. If he had gone to his older brother, things might have turned out differently.

The next questions are about how guilt and shame feel to you. They are not a test, and there is no score. Answer honestly, as a way into thinking and, if you wish, talking with someone you trust.

elements.text: Peter (I have changed some details) thought he had been a Christian for years. He went to church, and he believed Christianity was about being good enough for God. Then he truly understood the gospel, the good news about Jesus. He saw that he could not earn God’s favour, that he needed forgiveness, and that God freely offered it. So he prayed and asked God to rescue him.

elements.text: Titus 3 will help us to answer that question from the Bible’s perspective. Paul tells Titus to insist on ‘such truths’, so that believers will be intent on doing what is good. That would be a big step forward in godliness. The passage itself will tell us what the ‘truths’ are.

elements.passageText:
3For we too were once foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved to various passions and desires, spending our lives in evil and envy, hateful and hating one another. 4But “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared, 5he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, 6whom he poured out on us in full measure through Jesus Christ our Savior. 7And so, since we have been justified by his grace, we become heirs with the confident expectation of eternal life.”

8This saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on such truths, so that those who have placed their faith in God may be intent on engaging in good works. These things are good and beneficial for all people.

elements.question: Read verses 3–7. Jot down the key point being made in each verse.
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Take one verse at a time and note what it says about us or about God.
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 3 says we too were once foolish, disobedient, misled and enslaved to passions and desires. Verse 4 says God’s kindness and love for mankind appeared. Verse 5 says he saved us not by our works but on the basis of his mercy, through the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit. Verse 6 says he poured out the Spirit in full measure through Jesus Christ our Saviour. Verse 7 says we are justified by his grace and become heirs with the confident expectation of eternal life.

elements.question: What does Paul want these truths to lead to (verse 8)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Read verse 8 and notice what believers are to be intent on.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul wants Titus to insist on these truths so that those who have placed their faith in God will be intent on engaging in good works. The basic gospel is not only for the start of the Christian life; it is meant to shape how believers live. Paul calls these things good and beneficial for all people. So the gospel does not only make us Christians; it also makes us grow.

elements.text:
On one level this may be a surprise, because the whole paragraph is a basic summary of the gospel. But that is the point. Believing the gospel turns non-Christians into Christians, and that is true but not complete. The gospel also enables Christians to grow.

This is different from other areas of life. In maths, pupils do repetitive exercises to drill the basic ideas, and later they leave them behind and move on to more advanced work. Christianity is not like that. Paul tells Titus to keep stressing the basics, because they are good and beneficial for everyone. No matter how long we have been Christians, or how well we know our Bibles, we do not move on from the gospel. We come back to it again and again. The gospel saves you, but the gospel also makes you grow. Here is the first of three ways it does that.
Remember that sin destroys you

Proverbs 5:22–23

22The wicked will be captured by his own iniquities,
and he will be held by the cords of his own sin.
23He will die because there was no discipline;
because of the greatness of his folly he will reel.

Romans 6:16

16Do you not know that if you present yourselves as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one you obey, either of sin resulting in death, or obedience resulting in righteousness?

elements.question: How does sin trap and enslave the person who sins?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice the words ‘captured’, ‘cords’ and ‘slaves’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The wicked are captured by their own iniquities and held by the cords of their own sin, and the person without discipline dies because of his great folly. Romans 6:16 says that whoever presents himself as an obedient slave is a slave of the one he obeys: sin, resulting in death, or obedience, resulting in righteousness. Sin is not harmless; it traps people and becomes their master. The damage is done to the sinner, whom his own sin holds captive.

elements.passageText:
Proverbs 11:6

6The righteousness of the upright will deliver them,
but the treacherous will be ensnared by their own desires.

Galatians 5:16–17

16But I say, live by the Spirit and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh. 17For the flesh has desires that are opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires that are opposed to the flesh, for these are in opposition to each other, so that you cannot do what you want.

elements.question: What do these verses show about sin and our own desires?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Ask who is ensnared by desires, and how the flesh and the Spirit relate.
elements.sampleAnswer: Proverbs 11:6 says the treacherous are ensnared by their own desires, so our own desires can become the trap. Galatians 5:16–17 says the flesh has desires opposed to the Spirit, and the Spirit has desires opposed to the flesh. The two are in opposition, so that we cannot do what we want. Sin sets up a conflict inside us that damages us, unless we live by the Spirit.

elements.passageText:
1 Corinthians 6:18–20

18Flee sexual immorality! “Every sin a person commits is outside of the body” —but the immoral person sins against his own body. 19Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? 20For you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.

Isaiah 59:2

2But your sinful acts have alienated you from your God;
your sins have caused him to reject you and not listen to your prayers.

elements.question: How does sin damage the person who sins, and their relationship with God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at whom the immoral person sins against in 1 Corinthians, and what sin does in Isaiah.
elements.sampleAnswer: First Corinthians says the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit and we are not our own, because we were bought at a price. Isaiah 59:2 says that our sinful acts alienate us from God, and our sins cause him to reject us and not listen to our prayers. Sin harms us, and it harms our relationship with God.

elements.text:
The Bible’s picture of sin is like what it is like to take drugs. It can be great fun at first, which is why people do it. But it is an empty sort of fun. You need more and more to satisfy you, and in the end it never does satisfy. Sin entraps you and makes you its slave, in much the same way that people become enslaved to drugs. Sin destroys you.

The world thinks that by sinning it is throwing off bonds and liberating itself. That is not true. Sin dehumanises you. The more it works on you, the more it eats away at your humanity, and the more it turns you into a sort of spiritual drug addict. It happens quickly with some people and slowly with others, but it happens. You become more and more self-centred, and sin cuts you off from other people and from God. It will in the end destroy all your relationships, which is one of the most terrifying things about hell.

If we really understand that sin destroys us, we have a huge motive to devote ourselves to doing what is good. The next time you are tempted to do wrong, pause and remember the whole picture. Sin can be pleasurable; if it were not, we would not be tempted. But it is an empty pleasure which does us serious harm. Think twice.

elements.passageText:
Proverbs 13:6

6Righteousness guards the one who lives with integrity,
but wickedness overthrows the sinner.

Numbers 32:23

23“But if you do not do this, then look, you will have sinned against the Lord. And know that your sin will find you out.

James 1:15

15Then when desire conceives, it gives birth to sin, and when sin is full grown, it gives birth to death.

elements.question: Where does sin eventually lead us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Follow the steps in James 1:15, and notice what will ‘find you out’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Proverbs 13:6 says wickedness overthrows the sinner. Numbers 32:23 warns that your sin will find you out. James 1:15 shows the path: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and when sin is full grown it gives birth to death. Sin may begin as a desire that seems small, but it grows until it destroys. The end of the road is death.

elements.passageText:
Galatians 6:7–8

7Do not be deceived. God will not be made a fool. For a person will reap what he sows, 8because the person who sows to his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

Romans 6:23

23For the payoff of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

elements.question: What do we reap from sowing to the flesh and from sowing to the Spirit, and what is the gift of God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare the two kinds of sowing and their harvests.
elements.sampleAnswer: Galatians 6:7–8 says God will not be made a fool, and that a person reaps what he sows. Whoever sows to his own flesh will reap corruption, but whoever sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. Romans 6:23 says the payoff of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Sin pays its wages, but eternal life is a free gift.

elements.text: Titus 3 has more lessons to teach us.
Remember the mercy we don’t deserve

elements.passageText:
Titus 3:4–6

4But “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared, 5he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, 6whom he poured out on us in full measure through Jesus Christ our Savior.

Ephesians 2:4–5

4But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, 5even though we were dead in offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you are saved! —

elements.question: What do you learn in these verses about God’s mercy to us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice what moves God to save us, and what we contribute.
elements.sampleAnswer: In Titus 3:4–6 God saves us not by any righteous works of ours but on the basis of his mercy, when his kindness and love for mankind appeared. Ephesians 2:4–5 says God is rich in mercy, and because of his great love he made us alive together with Christ even though we were dead in offences. Mercy is something we do not deserve and cannot earn. It flows from God’s love and reaches us by grace.

elements.passageText:
Micah 7:18–19

18Who is a God like you?
Who forgives sin
and pardons the rebellion
of those who remain among his people?
Who does not stay angry forever,
but delights in showing loyal love?
19Who will once again have mercy on us?
Who will conquer our evil deeds?
Who will hurl all our sins into the depths of the sea?

Lamentations 3:22–23

22The Lord’s loyal kindness never ceases;
his compassions never end.
23They are fresh every morning;
your faithfulness is abundant!

elements.question: What do you learn in these verses about God’s mercy to us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what God does with our sin, and at the words ‘never’ and ‘every morning’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah says God forgives sin and pardons rebellion, does not stay angry for ever, and delights in showing loyal love. He will have mercy on us again and hurl all our sins into the depths of the sea. Lamentations says the Lord’s loyal kindness never ceases and his compassions never end. They are fresh every morning. God’s mercy is not used up or withdrawn, but is renewed every day.

elements.passageText: 16Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.

elements.question: What do you learn from this verse about God’s mercy to us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at how we are invited to come, and what we receive.
elements.sampleAnswer: We are invited to approach the throne of grace confidently. We come to receive mercy and to find grace whenever we need help. The throne is not a place where we are turned away, but where help is given. Mercy is there for us to receive, not to earn.

elements.text: We know we did not deserve to have God rescue us. But we can come to think that we must be good enough to stay in God’s good books. That is a dangerous lie, and like the best lies it twists the truth. It is true that if we are not growing in godliness, that suggests we may not really understand the gospel. But this is not a test to frighten you. Growth is uneven and not always easy to see. The question is not whether you have become good enough, but whether you are turning to Christ and trusting him to change you.

elements.passageText: 1From Paul, a slave of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, to further the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth that is in keeping with godliness,

elements.question: What does Paul expect a knowledge of the truth to lead to?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Read the end of the verse.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says the knowledge of the truth is in keeping with godliness. Truth and godliness go together. Knowing the gospel is meant to lead to a godly life, as it did for God’s chosen ones whose faith Paul wants to further. So if we understand the truth, it will change how we live.

elements.text: The truth leads to godliness. Understanding the gospel changes us. We never earn God’s mercy. We deserved condemnation for the lives we lived before we came to Christ, and we still deserve it for the lives we have lived since. But because we belong to Christ, God has forgiven us by his grace. If we want our lives changed, we need to understand more of the gospel.
Remember the whole New Creation

elements.passageText:
Titus 3:7

7And so, since we have been justified by his grace, we become heirs with the confident expectation of eternal life.”

Titus 2:13–14

13as we wait for the happy fulfillment of our hope in the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ. 14He gave himself for us to set us free from every kind of lawlessness and to purify for himself a people who are truly his, who are eager to do good.

elements.question: What do you learn about the New Creation we are heading for?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what we are waiting for, and at what Jesus is doing for his people.
elements.sampleAnswer: Because we are justified by grace, we become heirs with the confident expectation of eternal life. We are waiting for the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ, which is our happy hope. Jesus gave himself to set us free from lawlessness and to purify for himself a people who are truly his and eager to do good. The New Creation is where Christ’s rescue mission ends: a purified people with eternal life.

elements.passageText:
1Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had ceased to exist, and the sea existed no more. 2And I saw the holy city—the new Jerusalem—descending out of heaven from God, made ready like a bride adorned for her husband. 3And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Look! The residence of God is among human beings. He will live among them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. 4He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will not exist any more—or mourning, or crying, or pain, for the former things have ceased to exist.”

5And the one seated on the throne said: “Look! I am making all things new!” Then he said to me, “Write it down, because these words are reliable and true.”

elements.question: What do you learn about the New Creation we are heading for?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice who is with whom, and what has gone.
elements.sampleAnswer: There is a new heaven and a new earth, and the new Jerusalem comes down from God like a bride. God’s residence is among human beings, and he lives among his people. He wipes away every tear, and death, mourning, crying and pain are no more, for the former things have ceased. God says, ‘Look! I am making all things new!’ The New Creation is a world with God present and sin and its effects removed.

elements.passageText: 1Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life—water as clear as crystal—pouring out from the throne of God and of the Lamb, 2flowing down the middle of the city’s main street. On each side of the river is the tree of life producing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month of the year. Its leaves are for the healing of the nations. 3And there will no longer be any curse, and the throne of God and the Lamb will be in the city. His servants will worship him, 4and they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. 5Night will be no more, and they will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.

elements.question: What more do you learn about the New Creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look for what is present, and what will no longer be.
elements.sampleAnswer: The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life grows beside it, with leaves for the healing of the nations. There will no longer be any curse, and God’s servants will worship him. They will see his face, and the Lord God himself will be their light. They will reign for ever and ever. It is a life of unbroken closeness to God, with healing and blessing.

elements.text:
The goal of Jesus’ rescue mission is to purify a people for himself, completely free from sin. There are benefits to being a Christian now, but the best is still to come. The process of freeing us from the nightmare of sin has begun, but it is not finished. The New Creation is so good because we will be fully with God and fully without sin. We ourselves will be the opposite of the description in Titus 3:3. Holiness is not boring or bland. The New Creation will be wonderful because God will be there, and everyone else will be godly. Instead of living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another, we will live in kindness and peace, loving and caring for one another.

To sense the contrast between sin and godliness, look at the words Paul uses in Titus 3 for our two situations.

elements.passageText: 3For we too were once foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved to various passions and desires, spending our lives in evil and envy, hateful and hating one another. 4But “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared, 5he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, 6whom he poured out on us in full measure through Jesus Christ our Savior. 7And so, since we have been justified by his grace, we become heirs with the confident expectation of eternal life.”

elements.question: Pick out the words that describe our situation in sin (verse 3), and the words that describe God’s great rescue (verses 4–7).
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare verse 3 with verses 4–7.
elements.sampleAnswer: Our situation in sin is described as foolish, disobedient, misled, enslaved to passions and desires, living in evil and envy, hateful and hating one another. God’s rescue is described with kindness, love for mankind, mercy, the new birth and renewing of the Holy Spirit, justification by grace, and heirs with the expectation of eternal life. The contrast shows how far God has rescued us, from slavery and hatred to mercy, grace and hope.

elements.text: Physical idols were once common all over the world, and in some places they still are. When we hear the word ‘idol’, the picture that springs to mind is often a statue or an image. The Bible certainly uses the word that way, but it also uses ‘idol’ in other ways.

elements.passageText:
Exodus 20:4

4“You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above or that is on the earth beneath or that is in the water below.

Colossians 3:5

5So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry.

elements.question: What different forms of idolatry do these verses show us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare the carved image with the list in Colossians 3:5.
elements.sampleAnswer: Exodus 20:4 forbids making a carved image or any likeness of anything in heaven, on earth or in the water, so physical idols are one form of idolatry. Colossians 3:5 tells us to put to death sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire and greed, which is idolatry. So idolatry is not only a carved statue. Something like greed can be an idol too.

elements.passageText:
Psalm 115:4–8

4Their idols are made of silver and gold—
they are man-made.
5They have mouths, but cannot speak,
eyes, but cannot see,
6ears, but cannot hear,
noses, but cannot smell,
7hands, but cannot touch,
feet, but cannot walk.
They cannot even clear their throats.
8Those who make them will end up like them,
as will everyone who trusts in them.

Jeremiah 2:27–28

27They say to a wooden idol, ‘You are my father.’
They say to a stone image, ‘You gave birth to me.’
Yes, they have turned away from me instead of turning to me.
Yet when they are in trouble, they say, ‘Come and save us!’
28But where are the gods you made for yourselves?
Let them save you when you are in trouble.
The sad fact is that you have as many gods

elements.question: What do these verses say about idols, and about those who make and trust them?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice what idols cannot do, and what happens to the people who trust them.
elements.sampleAnswer: Psalm 115 says idols are man-made, of silver and gold. They have mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet that cannot work, and those who make and trust them end up like them. In Jeremiah 2 the people call a wooden idol their father, and then cry to God to save them when they are in trouble. God answers: let the gods you made save you. Idols are powerless, and trusting them leaves us helpless.

elements.passageText:
Ezekiel 14:3–4

3“Son of man, these men have erected their idols in their hearts and placed the obstacle leading to their iniquity right before their faces. Should I really allow them to seek me? 4Therefore speak to them and say to them, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord says: When anyone from the house of Israel erects his idols in his heart and sets the obstacle leading to his iniquity before his face, and then consults a prophet, I the Lord am determined to answer him personally according to the enormity of his idolatry.

Romans 1:21–25

21For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but they became futile in their thoughts and their senseless hearts were darkened. 22Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools 23and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for an image resembling mortal human beings or birds or four-footed animals or reptiles.

24Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity, to dishonor their bodies among themselves. 25They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.

elements.question: Where do idols take root, and what do people exchange for them?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at where Ezekiel says the idols are, and at what Romans says people exchange.
elements.sampleAnswer: Ezekiel says these men have erected their idols in their hearts and set the obstacle to their iniquity before their faces. So idols begin in the heart, and not only on a shelf. Romans 1 says people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for an image, and the truth of God for a lie. They worshipped and served the creation rather than the Creator. Idolatry is putting something created in the place of God.

elements.text: Idolatry is the worship or service of some created thing instead of the Creator. We take good things and wrongly centre our lives on them, turning them into ‘god-things’. That is when they become twisted and harmful.
Was Isaac Abraham’s idol?

elements.question: Imagine you are Abraham, waiting decades for the child of promise to arrive. How would you feel when the child is finally born?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your thoughts…

elements.passageText: 2God said, “Take your son—your only son, whom you love, Isaac —and go to the land of Moriah! Offer him up there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will indicate to you.”

elements.question: Now read what God says to Abraham. What does he ask, and how does he describe Isaac?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice the three descriptions God gives of Isaac.
elements.sampleAnswer: God asks Abraham to take his son and offer him as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. He describes Isaac as ‘your son’, ‘your only son’ and ‘whom you love’. These words stress how precious Isaac is. The request puts the gift and the Giver side by side, and asks which comes first.

elements.text: God calls Abraham to sacrifice Isaac. Why? Because idolatry is so dangerous. For Abraham, Isaac is certainly a ‘good thing’. He has waited his whole life for him, and all his hopes of blessing are tied up in the boy. If you had asked Abraham, ‘What is the greatest thing in your life?’ he might easily have said, ‘Isaac!’ But he should say, ‘God! And the biggest blessing he has given me is Isaac.’ The best things can become the greatest idols. God makes Abraham face a stark choice: God, or Isaac. Abraham chooses God, and that makes it safe for him to enjoy the blessing of his son without the blessing becoming an idol.
Why did Israel choose a golden calf?

Exodus 32 also tells a story of serious idolatry. God has redeemed Israel from slavery, they are at Mount Sinai, and God has spoken to them in the thunder. They have agreed that Moses should go up the mountain alone to receive the Law while they wait below. But then Moses is away a long time.

elements.passageText:
1When the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said to him, “Get up, make us gods that will go before us. As for this fellow Moses, the man who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him!”

2So Aaron said to them, “Break off the gold earrings that are on the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.” 3So all the people broke off the gold earrings that were on their ears and brought them to Aaron. 4He accepted the gold from them, fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made a molten calf. Then they said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.”

5When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it, and Aaron made a proclamation and said, “Tomorrow will be a feast to the Lord.” 6So they got up early on the next day and offered up burnt offerings and brought peace offerings, and the people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play.

7The Lord spoke to Moses, “Go quickly, descend, because your people, whom you brought up from the land of Egypt, have acted corruptly. 8They have quickly turned aside from the way that I commanded them—they have made for themselves a molten calf and have bowed down to it and sacrificed to it and said, ‘These are your gods, O Israel, which brought you up from the land of Egypt.’”

elements.question: How do the people respond when Moses is slow to return (verse 1)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Notice how they speak about Moses, and what they ask Aaron for.
elements.sampleAnswer: When the people see that Moses has delayed, they gather around Aaron. They tell him to make gods that will go before them. They speak of Moses as ‘this fellow’ and say they do not know what has become of him. God had rescued them from Egypt, yet they want something visible to lead them in place of the leader who has gone.

elements.text: Aaron tries to control the outburst of idol-making by asking for gold, which he makes into a ‘calf’. This is probably not a baby bull but a young bull. The idol does not stand for infancy, weakness or vulnerability. It stands for youthfulness, strength and vigour. That makes sense after their rescue from Egypt, where God had defeated a superpower, sent ten plagues and parted the Red Sea. Those were all acts of strength and power.

elements.question: What do the people say about the calf, and how does Aaron present the occasion (verses 4–6)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at what they say brought them out of Egypt, and what Aaron announces.
elements.sampleAnswer: Aaron collects their gold and makes a molten calf. The people say, ‘These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt’, giving the calf the credit for what God had done. Aaron builds an altar and announces a feast to the Lord. The next day they offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, and sit down to eat and drink and rise up to play. Aaron tries to dress up idolatry as worship of the Lord.

elements.text:
They are focusing on divine strength and power. But why do they say ‘gods’ and not ‘god’? Of course, they do not say it in English at all. The Hebrew word is ‘Elohim’, which can mean ‘God’, or ‘gods’. It is like the word ‘sheep’ in English: singular and plural look the same, so we say both ‘one sheep’ and ‘two sheep’. Here the Hebrew words for ‘these’ and for ‘brought up’ are plural, so it is natural to read ‘gods’, as the NET does.

Aaron still hopes to salvage something from this idolatry. He thinks he can turn it into a feast to ‘the Lord’ (Yahweh), with all the normal Old Testament burnt offerings and peace offerings. He is probably thinking something like: ‘We can work with this. Yahweh is strong. He rescued us from Egypt. A calf-idol is also strong, so it can represent Yahweh.’ But idol-worship is false worship.

elements.question: What is the Lord’s verdict on this ‘feast to the Lord’ (verses 7–8)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Read the Lord’s words to Moses, and note what the people have done.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord tells Moses to go down quickly because his people have acted corruptly. They have quickly turned aside from the way he commanded them. They have made a molten calf, bowed down to it and sacrificed to it, and said that it brought them out of Egypt. Calling it a feast to the Lord did not change what it really was: idolatry.

elements.text:
Words are important, but actions can be even more important. What we say we are doing matters, but what we are actually doing matters even more. Aaron said this was a feast ‘to the Lord’, but it was not; it was idolatry. Aaron did not realise that half-true, half-false worship of the true God is in fact false worship of God, which is worship of a false god. The Israelites probably said something like this: ‘God is strong! God is mighty and powerful! Our bull-calf expresses his strength. We serve the Almighty, and this image helps us focus on that truth.’

The true bits of this are not the problem. The problem is the false or twisted bits that sit alongside them, and the missing bits of truth that have been left out. It is not enough for something to have some truth. Half-truths are true as far as they go, but they are not the whole truth. The great thing about the Bible is that it gives us the whole truth, if we pay attention.

elements.text: Solomon’s story shows how idolatry can turn good things into ‘god-things’. Blessings can hold you back. His story starts well. God appears to him and asks him to choose a blessing.

elements.passageText: 7Now, O Lord my God, you have made your servant king in my father David’s place, even though I am only a young man and am inexperienced. 8Your servant stands among your chosen people; they are a great nation that is too numerous to count or number. 9So give your servant a discerning mind so he can make judicial decisions for your people and distinguish right from wrong. Otherwise no one is able to make judicial decisions for this great nation of yours.” 10The Lord was pleased that Solomon made this request. 11God said to him, “Because you asked for the ability to make wise judicial decisions, and not for long life, or riches, or vengeance on your enemies, 12I grant your request and give you a wise and discerning mind superior to that of anyone who has preceded or will succeed you. 13Furthermore, I am giving you what you did not request—riches and honor so that you will be the greatest king of your generation. 14If you follow my instructions by obeying my rules and regulations, just as your father David did, then I will grant you long life.”

elements.question: What does Solomon ask for, and what else does God give him?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare what Solomon asks for in verse 9 with what God adds in verses 13–14.
elements.sampleAnswer: Solomon asks for a discerning mind so that he can make judicial decisions for God’s people and distinguish right from wrong. God is pleased, and gives him a wise and discerning mind superior to anyone before or after him. Because Solomon did not ask for long life, riches or vengeance, God also gives him riches and honour, so that he will be the greatest king of his generation. God promises long life as well, if Solomon obeys his rules and regulations as David did.

elements.text: Soon the blessings are fulfilled. Solomon rules wisely, and he has peace, wealth and fame. Even the Queen of Sheba comes to see his court.

elements.passageText: 6She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own country about your wise sayings and insight was true! 7I did not believe these things until I came and saw them with my own eyes. Indeed, I didn’t hear even half the story! Your wisdom and wealth surpass what was reported to me. 8Your attendants, who stand before you at all times and hear your wise sayings, are truly happy! 9May the Lord your God be praised because he favored you by placing you on the throne of Israel! elements.sampleAnswer: She says the report she heard was true, and that she did not believe it until she saw it with her own eyes. She is impressed by Solomon’s wisdom and wealth, which surpass what she was told. She says his attendants, who hear his wise sayings, must be truly happy. She praises the Lord, who favoured Solomon and made him king so that he could make just and right decisions.

elements.text: The picture we are given of Solomon’s court is bright, beautiful and glorious. And yet we know that it all falls apart so quickly.

elements.passageText: 9The Lord was angry with Solomon because he had shifted his allegiance away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him on two occasions 10and had warned him about this very thing, so that he would not follow other gods. But he did not obey the Lord’s command.

elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage

elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord is angry with Solomon because he has shifted his allegiance away from the Lord. The Lord had appeared to him twice and had warned him not to follow other gods. But Solomon did not obey the Lord’s command. The man who began by asking for wisdom ends up following other gods.

elements.text: How did it all fall apart so quickly? The cracks were there much earlier. Consider what God said, in advance, about how Israel’s kings were to conduct themselves.

elements.sampleAnswer: The king must not accumulate horses for himself. He must not allow the people to return to Egypt to get more horses. He must not marry many wives, in case his affections turn aside. And he must not accumulate much silver and gold.

elements.text: Solomon does not do well on these four counts. Even in 1 Kings 10, where things are going so well, they are at the same time going very badly. The verses below are the ones that deal with horses, Egypt, gold and silver, and wives.

elements.passageText:
14Solomon received 666 talents of gold per year, 15besides what he collected from the merchants, traders, Arabian kings, and governors of the land.

23King Solomon was wealthier and wiser than any of the kings of the earth.

26Solomon accumulated chariots and horses. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses. He kept them in assigned cities and in Jerusalem. 27The king made silver as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones; cedar was as plentiful as sycamore fig trees are in the foothills. 28Solomon acquired his horses from Egypt and from Que; the king’s traders purchased them from Que. 29They paid 600 silver pieces for each chariot from Egypt and 150 silver pieces for each horse. They also sold chariots and horses to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Syria.

11:1King Solomon fell in love with many foreign women (besides Pharaoh’s daughter), including Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites.

3He had 700 royal wives and 300 concubines; his wives had a powerful influence over him. 4When Solomon became old, his wives shifted his allegiance to other gods; he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord his God, as his father David had been. 5Solomon worshiped the Sidonian goddess Astarte and the detestable Ammonite god Milcom. 6Solomon did evil in the Lord’s sight; he did not remain loyal to the Lord, as his father David had.

elements.question: How does Solomon do on each of the four requirements: horses, Egypt, gold and silver, and wives?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Take each requirement in turn and look for it in the verses.
elements.sampleAnswer: Solomon accumulates horses on a huge scale: he has 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses. His horses are imported from Egypt, so he breaks the second requirement as well. He breaks the third: he receives 666 talents of gold a year and makes silver as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones. He breaks the fourth: he has 700 royal wives and 300 concubines, who shift his allegiance to other gods. Solomon fails on all four, even while things seem to be going so well.

elements.text:
Despite all the blessings Solomon receives, he goes astray. Sin twists the blessings into idols. Solomon delights in wealth, power and status so much that he puts them ahead of God. He should have received his blessings from God and used them in service to God, even when that meant putting God ahead of the blessings.

Our hopes and dreams give clues about our idols. We think our idols will bring us satisfaction: ‘If only I were wealthy (or married, or successful), everything would be all right!’ It is not wrong to hope for blessings; they are good things. The problem begins when we stop seeing them as gifts from the Saviour and start treating them as our salvation.

Our fears and worries also give clues. Fear shows us where we look for security and meaning. That makes us vulnerable, because idols are only created things, and created things can be lost. If you lose something good, you will grieve, and that is right. Grief can make life feel empty for a time, and that does not mean you made an idol of what you lost. But if you find, over a long time, that you cannot see any hope without that thing, it is worth asking whether it had become more than a gift.

If you are grieving now, please hear this: grief is not idolatry, and this study is not an accusation. Grieve, and talk to someone you trust. If grief ever leaves you thinking of ending your life, tell a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor today.

God can use hard times to show us where our trust has gone wrong. But we cannot assume that a particular loss happened for that reason, and a loss is never proof that you did something wrong.

elements.text:
If you are turning a blessing into an idol, you have three paths:

  1. You repent. You turn from the idol and refocus on God, even if that means holding it more loosely for a time. In time, you may be able to enjoy it as a blessing and not as an idol.
  2. You carry on worshipping it. It keeps its hold on you, and you may pay a high price, until you see it, repent and turn back to him.
  3. You carry on worshipping it, and God lets you. It pulls you further from him, and the damage can be deep.

What will you choose? The wise choice is the first path. No one else can choose it for you. You would be wise to start today.

elements.text: Wisdom is the ability to apply knowledge and understanding to life, at the right time and in the right way.
The beginning of wisdom

elements.passageText:
10The beginning of wisdom is to fear the Lord,
and acknowledging the Holy One is understanding.

elements.question: Where does wisdom begin?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Look at the first line of the verse.
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse says the beginning of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and that acknowledging the Holy One is understanding. So wisdom starts with who we know, and not only with what we know. It begins with taking God seriously and knowing him. Without that beginning, cleverness is not the same as wisdom.

elements.text: Wisdom starts with who you know, that is, God, and not just with what you know. Knowing God should shape our every thought, decision and action. To be wise, we need to know God, the Creator of the universe. We need to fear him, and we need to learn his ways.

elements.passageText:
7Fearing the Lord is the beginning of discernment,
but fools have despised wisdom and moral instruction.
16:16How much better it is to acquire wisdom than gold;
to acquire understanding is more desirable than silver.

elements.question: How important is it to gain and grow in wisdom?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Compare wisdom with gold and silver, and notice what fools do with it.
elements.sampleAnswer: Proverbs 1:7 says fearing the Lord is the beginning of discernment, but fools despise wisdom and moral instruction. Proverbs 16:16 says it is much better to acquire wisdom than gold, and that understanding is more desirable than silver. Wisdom is worth more than wealth. Despising wisdom is the mark of a fool.

elements.text: You need some wisdom to use wisdom
It is a little ironic that you need to use some wisdom in order to gain more of it. Consider these two proverbs.

elements.passageText:
4Do not answer a fool according to his folly,
lest you yourself also be like him.
5Answer a fool according to his folly,
lest he be wise in his own opinion.

elements.question: How should we respond to someone who is being foolish? Why do these two proverbs seem to disagree?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Try to answer the question from the Bible passage
elements.questionHint: Read the reason each verse gives after the word ‘lest’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Proverbs 26:4 says not to answer a fool according to his folly, or you will become like him. Proverbs 26:5 says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own opinion. The two proverbs seem to disagree, but each fits a different situation. Sometimes we should walk away so as not to be dragged down; at other times the best way to show a foolish idea for what it is may be to respond in kind. We need wisdom to see which proverb fits the situation in front of us.
keyTerms: not to answer|do not answer|not answer

elements.text: These two proverbs are placed side by side to get us thinking. There are times when you need to avoid being dragged into foolish discussions, or you will be pulled down to that level. There are other times when the best way of pointing out foolishness is to play along with it and respond in kind. The proverbs teach us wisdom by naming both situations. But we still need wisdom to recognise which proverb fits the situation in front of us. Wisdom is like a ladder: you use wisdom to learn more wisdom.
