introduction.body:
This chapter goes with Studies 8 and 9.

‘As Scripture says, “Anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame.”’ (Romans 10:11)

Have you ever felt so ashamed about something that you never wanted to talk about it, and never wanted anyone to know? Luka felt like that. His story is true, and he has agreed to my telling it. I have changed his name. He had been secretly struggling with pornography use for ten years – since his early teens. He had never spoken to anyone about it, and felt he never could. He had tried to stop on his own, and sometimes had managed – for a week or two. But he always fell back into the trap. No matter how hard he tried, no matter how much fasting or praying he did, the problem wouldn’t seem to go away. He needed help – but he was too ashamed to ask for help.

What would you tell Luka? What advice would you give? There are two problems in giving him advice. The easier problem is what you should say. The harder problem is that you don’t even know you should say anything – because he is too ashamed to ask anyone. Perhaps you know what this feels like from the inside, because of having been in a similar situation in the past. Perhaps you are in a similar situation now.

We need to think through the negative effects of shame, how they hold us back, and how we can overcome them.

theProblemOfShame.body:
Before we go on, it helps to say what shame is. Guilt says, ‘I did something wrong.’ Shame says, ‘I am wrong.’ Ed Welch describes shame as ‘the deep sense that you are unacceptable because of something you did, something done to you, or something associated with you’.[[fn:1]]

Human beings were designed for honour, but sin twists that out of shape. Sin brings us dishonour – shame – but it also deceives us into seeking honour in the wrong places. The early chapters of Genesis give us a brief glimpse of how life should have been – a life without shame:

Adam and his wife were both naked, and they felt no shame. (Genesis 2:25)

But we have lost that world. After the Fall, humans easily experience shame. And we do not like it. We realise that we all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and – like Adam and Eve – we want to find some ‘fig leaves’ to cover up our shame. But fig leaves are full of holes and gaps; they don’t make good coverings. And that tends to lead to trouble. One kind of trouble is that we can try to distract from our own shame by bringing shame on someone else.

Shame often leads to more shame. When we feel ashamed, we try to feel bigger by making someone else smaller. Gossip, bullying, violence, abuse and hatred of other tribes are some of the ways we do it. We lift ourselves up by pushing others down, and we pass our shame on.[[fn:2]] Sin often works like this – it multiplies. Followers of Jesus should see at once that this is wrong. It goes against what God wants for his family.

Shame damages God’s family in many ways. Four things go together: sin dishonours God; sin makes us truly shameful before him; sin leaves us feeling ashamed; and shame pushes us into more sin.

Think again of the story of the prodigal son in Luke 15. The younger son brings much shame into his family. His initial request for the inheritance is shameful. The way he wastes his money in the foreign land is shameful. When it runs out he finds himself in a shameful condition: moneyless, tending unclean animals, and longing to eat their food!

But to go back home and beg for mercy is also shameful – perhaps even more shameful. In the distant land he is among strangers. His shame is ‘shallower’ precisely because it is happening among strangers. But if he returns home – the shame will be ‘deep’. He will be shamed before his family, his friends, and everyone who has known him from childhood onwards.

And he knows he has no claim on anything. He has wasted his inheritance, shamed his family, and forfeited his right to be called a son. He admits as much to himself:

18I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants. (Luke 15:18-19)

He does something right here. He realises that he has brought shame on himself and he stops pretending and hiding. He humbles himself and realises there is nothing he can do to fix things. That’s an important insight. You cannot lift yourself out of the swamp of shame. If there is going to be any way out, then someone else – someone honourable – has to reach down into the swamp and lift you out. It never occurs to the younger son that this might happen, but it is exactly what the father does. The father does not stand on his honour, and does not seek to underline the son’s shame. The father sets aside his honour and runs to the younger son and embraces him, shame and all. The father reaches down into the son’s shame, and lifts him out.

The father is a picture of God’s grace to us in Christ, and a picture of the same grace that Jesus wants us to show one another.

Jesus lived among people who cared deeply about honour and shame. He reached out to those who were shamed. He challenged those who pushed others down to raise themselves. And he called his followers to live differently, even when that set them against what everyone around them thought was honourable.

To follow Jesus in this way will often mean going against the ‘right’ and ‘proper’ ways of behaving that our world teaches us. It will often mean doing things that others think are not ‘respectable’. Our world, of course, is more like the older brother in the parable. He understands the ‘normal’ rules of honour and shame. The younger son has acted shamefully and so has forfeited his honour – his honour is gone, it is destroyed, there is no way to get it back. The younger son will just have to live with his shame. More than that, the younger son ought to have to live with his shame. It is what should happen – he should be shamed, and it is his family’s duty to shame him. In the older son’s eyes, the father is short-circuiting the ‘natural justice’ of the world.

In the world’s code, an insult must be answered. Revenge is meant to win honour back, but it only starts a cycle of violence. Jesus taught the opposite: love your enemies and do not hit back (Matthew 5:38-48). And he did not only teach it. He lived it, all the way to the cross.

The irony is that the older son in his anger also behaves shamefully towards his father, and dishonours his father by refusing to join the party or even enter the house – though in his anger he does not notice this. His father responds to him with equal grace, ignoring the dishonour, and going out to speak with the older son. The story ends without us seeing how the older son will respond to the father’s grace. Grace feels like a gamble, because the father cannot make either son accept it. The open ending leaves us, as the audience, to make the choice for ourselves. Will we follow the world’s code of shaming the shameful, and honouring the outwardly-honourable (even when they are inwardly shameful)? Or will we follow God’s radical reversal? Will we openly acknowledge our own shame (whether hidden or not), humble ourselves before God, and be welcomed by him, and lifted up?

God’s way of dealing with honour and shame is almost the exact opposite of the world’s way: the first will be last, and the last will be first (Matthew 20:16); he will lift up the lowly, but bring down the proud (Luke 1:52). The following table tries to capture that reversal. It shows the world’s code of honour in its usual form. Human cultures differ, and many also honour humility and service:

Human cultureGod’s Kingdom
ShamedShowing humility,
putting others first & serving others		Honoured
HonouredShowing pride,
being a ‘big man’
& being served		Shamed

If your sense of who you are is not built securely on the fact that you are precious to God and loved by him – if you are not confident that you are honoured by God and treasured by him – then (like the older son) you will look for honour and security through worldly shortcuts. And those shortcuts will cut across other people, and be at their expense. You will build yourself up – but it will be at the expense of pulling other people down. Our world builds whole communities like this – and sometimes our church communities do it too. We create an artificial version of ourselves – photoshopped to make it as ‘glorious’ and impressive as possible – and we hide our true selves behind this mask-person. We exchange the possibility of true community – where our true selves know one another and are known – and we replace it with an artificial ‘mask-community’ of mask-persons talking to other mask-persons. We exchange real relationships for artificial mask-relationships.

Being confident in God’s love for you will give you the confidence to know that you cannot win your own glory and honour – indeed, that you have forfeited your own honour through your sin – and yet, if you trust in Christ, you are honoured anyway! God has chosen you to be his child, and has adopted you into his family. You are a co-heir with Christ (Romans 8:17). You are precious to the Almighty God of all the universe. You have real honour through Jesus. If you are confident in his love, you can be confident in this; if you forget about his love for you, you may also forget about how honoured you are in him.

And if you forget about that – the honour that Jesus gives you, which washes away the shame you have earned by your sin – then you may start looking for substitutes in all the wrong places. You may forget about the real honour you have in Christ, and go looking for false honour elsewhere.

One of the ways sin messes up our thinking is that we confuse the reality of honour with the illusion of honour. I remember talking to Uche, whom we met in Chapter 2. He is a different man from Luka. Uche had fallen into sexual immorality (including abortion). He was in a relationship that was pulling him further and further into sin, but he was not sure how to get out because his girlfriend had said that if he ended the relationship, she would tell everyone what they had done. He didn’t want that to happen because, he was telling himself, he was a youth leader in his church and he ‘didn’t want to let everyone down’.

This is where sin can deceive us again. The simple fact is that the honour he was guarding was not real, because he already knew what he had done. And by covering up the earlier sin, he was allowing himself to be drawn into further sin, and was letting everyone down even more. He was confusing the reality of honour (which involves doing the right thing and being honoured for it) with the illusion of honour (which involves doing the wrong thing, but being honoured as if you had done the right thing, because no one has noticed the problem yet). It can also happen the other way round: people are sometimes shamed when they have done nothing wrong. We come back to this later in this chapter.

In our mixed-up world, you can sometimes get away with the illusion of honour for quite a while – but not for ever. Even in our fallen world, truth has a way of coming out. And even if it doesn’t come out in your lifetime – which can happen – there are still two very serious problems: (i) God knows – he knows from the very start, and his view of us matters more than the world’s view; (ii) a day is coming when all things will be brought to light – we will all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), to give an account of how we have lived, and all secrets will be brought into the open (Luke 12:2). There is real honour to be found in confronting our sin, and the shame that goes with it, repenting and learning again to follow Jesus faithfully. There is no real honour in covering over our sin and shame, and failing to repent properly because we want to hang onto the false honour of our false reputation.

gainingConfidenceThatOurHonourIsFoundInG.header: Gaining Confidence That Our Honour Is Found in God
gainingConfidenceThatOurHonourIsFoundInG.body:
Take some moments to read through each of the following verses, and meditate on them. I’m going to suggest that you follow this simple procedure:

  • Read a single verse.

  • Meditate on it for at least 30 seconds, longer if you can. Think through what it means. Ask yourself whether you have come to accept the truth that it expresses. Do you ‘own’ that truth? Has that truth come to shape your thinking?

  • Pray briefly about the verse. Ask God to help you to ‘own’ it (or to help you go on ‘owning’ it).

Here are the verses – meditate on each of them:[[fn:3]]

  • My salvation and my honour depend on God; he is my mighty rock, my refuge. (Psalm 62:7)

  • He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap; he seats them with princes and makes them inherit a throne of honour. (1 Samuel 2:8)

  • For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. (Hebrews 12:2)

  • And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death – even death on a cross! Therefore God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name. (Philippians 2:8-9)

  • I have given them the glory that you gave me, that they may be one as we are one. (John 17:22)

  • But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. (1 Peter 2:9-10)

areThereAnyPositiveBenefitsFromShame.header: Are There Any Positive Benefits from Shame?
areThereAnyPositiveBenefitsFromShame.body:
Sometimes people suggest that there are positive benefits from shame – specifically that it discourages us from doing the wrong thing, so that we won’t feel ashamed of ourselves afterwards. There may be some truth to this. In advance of wrongdoing, shame may function as a useful deterrent – not always a strong deterrent, but a useful one.

However, the problem flips right round once the wrongdoing has happened. From a gospel point of view, the right response to falling into sin is confession, repentance and forgiveness. The right response is to humble yourself (like the prodigal son) and then receive God’s grace. He lifts up the lowly. But from the world’s perspective, the lowly are to be kept low. That means that from a worldly honour-shame perspective, yes, the first choice is to do the right thing and avoid the wrong thing. But the next choice, if you have already done wrong, is to cover it up. Deny all wrongdoing, pretend it never happened, blame someone else, cover it up at all costs. From a worldly point of view, the last option is to confess. If you confess, you lose face; if you confess, you lose status; if you confess, you lose honour and gain shame.

This puts the world’s honour-values in direct confrontation with God’s honour-values. We can capture this in another table:

How do you respond when you have sinned?

Human cultureGod’s Kingdom
Rejection, Blame, ShameConfess your sin; Repent; Seek forgiveness.Acceptance, Forgiveness, Honour
Acceptance, Status, HonourDeny your sin,
Cover it up
Blame someone else		Rejection, Blame, Shame

That means that when you have done wrong, you need to decide whose approval you will live for. You cannot impress both the world and God. You will need to choose one. That choice matters, because the world’s ‘honour’ will not last, and nor will its shame. God’s view is the one that lasts for ever (Daniel 12:2 speaks of the final verdict: everlasting life, or shame and everlasting contempt).

Not all shame comes from our own sin. If someone has abused you or wronged you, the shame you feel is not yours to carry, and you do not need to confess it as sin. You may go on feeling it for a while, even when you know it was not your fault. That is common, and healing takes time and help. Tell a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust, and read ‘If Someone Sinned against You’ in Chapter 12. The same is true if someone is threatening you: you do not have to face that alone.

If you are ministering to someone like Luka – or if you find yourself in a position like his, of being trapped by shame – then there is only one good way out:

3When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.
4For day and night your hand was heavy on me;
my strength was sapped as in the heat of summer.

5Then I acknowledged my sin to you and did not cover up my iniquity.
I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the Lord.’
And you forgave the guilt of my sin. (Psalm 32:3-5)

We should confess our sins to God, and also to one another:

Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. (James 5:16)

God does not expect us to carry the burden of sin and shame alone. He expects us to carry one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2), to support one another, and to show his grace to one another. Choose one person who is mature and trustworthy, usually of your own sex. If you are attracted to people of your own sex, look first for a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust. We say more about this in Chapters 11 and 13. The prodigal son did well to go to his father. If he had gone to his older brother, things might have turned out differently.

Trustworthy means safe: someone who will treat you with dignity and keep what you say private, unless someone is in danger (Chapter 11 says more). You choose how much to say, and telling one person is not the same as telling everyone. If someone trusts you with their secret, receive them as the father received his son. Do not shame them, and do not press them to say more than they choose.

backToLuka.body:
Luka did find, in the end, a safe place to ask for help. It did not solve his struggle at once. But it was a turning point, and it set him on a path towards change.

What would I tell anyone in his place? First, that shame is not a reason to stay silent. The Father runs towards people who are ashamed. Second, that hiding feeds shame, and the way out is to tell God, and then one mature, trustworthy person. Third, that your worth is not decided by your worst secret. In Christ you are already honoured. And fourth, that falling again is not the end. We turn again, as Chapter 11 says, and Chapter 12 speaks to the struggle Luka faced.

keyPoints.body:
• Guilt says, ‘I did wrong.’ Shame says, ‘I am wrong.’ Both need the gospel.

  • Sin twists our desire for honour. We hide, or we lift ourselves up by pushing others down.

  • Like the younger son, we cannot lift ourselves out of shame. The Father reaches down and lifts us out.

  • In Christ we are already honoured. We are God’s children and co-heirs with Christ.

  • The world says hide your sin. God says confess it, to him and to one mature person you trust. Shame from what was done to us is not ours to confess.

puttingItIntoPractice.body: This week, choose one thing you have done wrong and have been hiding. Tell God about it, using Psalm 32:5 if it helps. Then decide who you will tell: one mature, trustworthy person, usually of your own sex, who will treat you with dignity and keep what you say private. You choose how much to say. If you are attracted to people of your own sex, begin with a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust. If it was done to you, you do not need to confess it. Tell a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust. If the first person you tell does not believe you or blames you, that is not your failure. Try someone else.

questionsForReflection.body:
• As you think it through, which should you give more importance to: being honoured in the sight of God, or being honoured in the sight of the world?

  • As you think about how you actually live, which do you give more importance to in practice: being honoured in the sight of God, or being honoured in the sight of the world?

  • Is there anything in your life at present that you are ashamed of, and covering up, and need to confess?

  • It is good to confess to God, and it is good to confess to one another. Do you have someone you can confess your sins and problems to?

  • Is some of the shame you carry from something that was done to you? Who could you talk to about that – a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor you trust?

introduction.body:
This chapter goes with Studies 10 and 11.

‘He saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy.’ (Titus 3:5)

I have a friend, I’ll call him Peter (I have changed some details), who became a Christian a while ago. He thought he’d been a Christian for years – he’d certainly been going to church for years – and he thought Christianity was about living a good life so that God would be pleased and let him into heaven. Then, for the first time, he really understood the gospel – the good news about Jesus. He realised that he could never earn his way into God’s favour, that he needed to be forgiven, and that God was offering to do just that. So he prayed to God, asking God to rescue him.

The question I would like you to think about is this: now that Peter has understood the gospel and has committed his life to God, what should be the next thing that he needs to find out about? Now that he’s finally got to grips with the gospel and become a Christian what does he need to move on to next, to learn how to live a life which pleases God? Take a moment to think about that – what’s the next thing he should move on to? – and to make it specific, jot your answer down in your notebook.

There’s a verse in Titus 3 that will help us to give an answer from the Bible’s perspective:

This is a trustworthy saying. And I want you to stress these things, so that those who have trusted in God may be careful to devote themselves to doing what is good. These things are excellent and profitable for everyone. (Titus 3:8)

Obviously we will need more context to understand this verse well, especially what the ‘these things’ are. But before we turn to that context, there is something very important to notice, namely this: Paul tells Titus to stress ‘these things’ precisely because they will encourage Christians ‘to devote themselves to doing what is good’. And being devoted to doing what is good would be a big step forward in growing in godliness. So we should look back to find out what ‘these things’ are. We will start from Titus 3:3:

3At one time we too were foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. We lived in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. 4But when the kindness and love of God our Saviour appeared, 5he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, 6whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Saviour, 7so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs having the hope of eternal life. 8This is a trustworthy saying. And I want you to stress these things, so that those who have trusted in God may be careful to devote themselves to doing what is good. These things are excellent and profitable for everyone. (Titus 3:3-8)

Now on one level this might be a surprise, because the whole paragraph is simply a basic summary of the gospel. But that is crucial to understand; it is the main idea I want to get at. Certainly the gospel turns non-Christians into Christians – that is true, but it is not complete. The gospel doesn’t just turn non-Christians into Christians, the gospel also makes Christians grow.

This is very different from a lot of areas in life. Take maths for example. I used to be a maths teacher, and when I was teaching something new I would normally make the pupils do lots of repetitive little exercises, over and over, so as to get them used to the basic concepts. And then later, if things went well, we were able to leave those behind and move on to more advanced stuff. The introductory exercises weren’t the main point, they just got you going. When you mastered them, you left them behind. Or when you are learning to play the piano, what you really want is to get to play the Moonlight Sonata or a Mozart concerto (or perhaps something more modern and popular). On the way you may have to learn chords and scales and arpeggios and such things. But they are just basics. They are not the real thing, and you can’t wait to move on from them.

But it is not like that with Christianity. Paul tells Titus to stress the basics of Christianity and to keep on stressing them. They are excellent and profitable for everybody. No matter how long we have been Christians, no matter how well we know our Bibles, we don’t move on from the gospel. We need to keep on coming back to the gospel again and again. The gospel saves you but the gospel also makes you grow.

But it is important to understand how that works. So we are going to think about how exactly it is that the gospel makes us grow. We will look at three examples, and all of them are about remembering the whole picture.

rememberTheWholePictureSinDestroysYou.header: Remember the Whole Picture – Sin Destroys You
rememberTheWholePictureSinDestroysYou.body:
At one time we too were foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. We lived in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. (Titus 3:3)

That is a description of my friend Peter, and indeed of everybody, before they come to Christ. It is very strong stuff. Imagine your pastor came up to you after church one day, and told you that by nature you are foolish and disobedient. And deceived, and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. Imagine they told you that without Christ you would be living in malice and envy, being hated and hating other people. I am not sure what you would think. I guess at the very least you would think that pastor was extraordinarily rude.

But it is true. Without Christ this is what we are all like. Sin is the word the Bible uses to describe this ugly state of affairs. It does not mean that everyone is always as malicious as they can possibly be. Not at all. By God’s grace there is still much good in the world, and in people, even before we come to Jesus. But the truth is that we live in a fallen world. A world marked by malice and envy and hatred. It is not just the world ‘out there’ that is marked – we ourselves are marked by those things. And even after we come to Christ, that sin is still part of us. We are forgiven, and its rule over us is broken – Christ makes an enormous difference – but sin is not yet banished. Not this side of the New Creation.

This picture we get in verse 3 of sin is similar to what it is like to take heroin – it can be great fun at first, that is why people do it. But it is an empty sort of fun. You need more and more to satisfy you – and in the end it never really does satisfy. Sin entraps you and makes you its slave in much the same way that people get enslaved and addicted to drugs. Sin destroys you. That would be true for us without Christ. The same is true for the people we meet at work, the people we pass when we are out shopping, everybody. Everybody rejects God. We do it by nature – that is how deeply sin has infected us. With some people it is blatant and obvious that they reject God, but it is true even when people are nice and polite and middle class – everyone who is living in God’s world without acknowledging him as king is disobedient.

And the thing is – that is a foolish way to live. If someone follows that path, then just like my friend Peter, they are deceived; maybe deceived into thinking ‘I live a good life, I’ll be OK’, or maybe deceived into thinking it doesn’t matter how they live. But those are all lies. In the future they will face God’s judgment, and in the present they are enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures – whether they have the self-understanding to see it or not, whether they are prepared to admit it or not.

The world likes to think that by sinning it is throwing off all sorts of legalistic and repressive bonds and liberating itself, but it is not true. Sin dehumanises you. The more it gets to work on you, the more it eats away at your humanity, the more it turns you into a sort of spiritual drug addict. It happens very quickly with some people, and it happens much more slowly with others. But either way it still happens. You become more and more self-centred, and it alienates you from other people and from God. And it will eventually destroy all your relationships with everybody, which is one of the most solemnly terrifying things about hell. If we really understand that sin destroys us, then we have a tremendous motive to devote ourselves to doing what is good. The next time you are tempted to do something wrong – pause. Pause for a moment and remember the whole picture. Sure, sin can be pleasurable – if it wasn’t then we wouldn’t be tempted so much. But it is empty pleasure which does us serious, serious harm. Think twice.

Incidentally, if we understand this verse properly, it also completely changes the way we see people who are not Christians. There is a danger that as we were looking at verse 3, we could miss the point and end up thinking ‘Aren’t we Christians so much better than those people who don’t know God.’ There is a danger of us looking at the moral failure of others and giving ourselves a rather proud pat on the back. But verse 3 should produce exactly the opposite reaction. Look at Titus 3:1:

Remind the people to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready to do whatever is good, to slander no one, to be peaceable and considerate, and always to be gentle towards everyone. [Because][[fn:1]] at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. We lived in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. (Titus 3:1-3)

There is a lot packed into what Paul says in verses 1-2 about how we should live, and it would be worth spending considerable time looking at it. But for now, all we will do is pick out the link between verses 2 and 3. Paul says that we should act in true humility towards all people because at one time we too were just as bad as anyone else. As Christians we can look at the modern equivalents of tax-collectors and the worst of sinners – drug-dealers, terrorists, rapists – and say without any exaggeration: ‘There go I, but for the grace of God’. This does not excuse what they have done, or make the harm any less. It means that we too depend entirely on God’s grace. So, remember the whole picture – remember that sin destroys you.

rememberTheWholePictureRememberTheMercyW.header: Remember the Whole Picture – Remember the Mercy We Don’t Deserve
rememberTheWholePictureRememberTheMercyW.body:
As well as remembering the negatives, we should remember the positives. Look at verse 4 again:

But when the kindness and love of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Saviour. (Titus 3:4-6)

Verse 5 is the heart of this section, and indeed the heart of the gospel: ‘he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy.’ That is exactly what my friend Peter didn’t understand before he became a Christian, and it seems to be what many people misunderstand about Christianity. The fact is that it is bad people who get into the New Creation, not good people. None of us are good enough for God’s New Creation. We all deserve to be banished for the way that we have lived – the Bible calls that place of banishment ‘hell’ – and it is not a good outcome. We have all rebelled against God: before we became Christians, some of us didn’t want anything to do with him. Others of us went along with him, but only when it suited us. For many of us he was the last thing we wanted to be bothered with. And if at any point we did deal with him, we were going to make sure it was on our terms, not his. God would have been justified in banishing us, there and then. But what did he do? Verse 5 – he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. And I guess that if we are Christians, we know this is true of us. We didn’t deserve to have God rescue us. But there is a danger that even though we know we didn’t deserve to be made right with God at the start, we begin thinking we have to reach a certain level of goodness to earn the right to stay in God’s good books.

That is a dangerous lie, and like all the best lies, it takes something that is true and twists it completely out of shape. Because it is true to say that if we are not living a Christian life – if we are not growing in godliness – then that strongly suggests that perhaps we don’t really understand the gospel, and that we may not really be Christians. This is not a test to frighten you. Growth is uneven, as we saw in the introduction, and it is not always easy to see. The question is not whether you have become good enough, but whether you are turning to Christ and trusting him to change you. If you are afraid that you are not growing, and you want to, come back to the gospel today. God welcomes everyone who comes to him. Look back to Titus 1:1, ‘Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ to further the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness.’ The truth leads to godliness. If we understand the gospel then it will change our lives. But that is very different from saying that we have to earn the right to stay in God’s good books. We deserved to be condemned for the lives we lived before we became Christians, and we still deserve to be condemned for the lives that we have lived since. But we are not condemned. Because we belong to Christ, God has forgiven us by his grace, and not because we have become good enough (Romans 8:1). There is no room for the moral arrogance of thinking that we deserve to stay right with God, whereas other people clearly don’t. We’re all sinners saved by God’s mercy. That means we don’t deserve it and we never will. If we understand the gospel then it will change our lives more and more. And if we want our lives to be changed then we need to understand the gospel more and more.

Perhaps you have never heard the name Philip Lawrence. There is no reason why you should. He was the headteacher of a school in London. One day in December 1995 a gang came to the school gates to attack one of his pupils. Philip Lawrence went out to help the boy, and he was stabbed. He died of his wounds.[[fn:2]]

Now I don’t know what you thought of your headteacher when you were at school. I used to think mine was dull, irrelevant, badly dressed, out of date, a bit of a nuisance, and a bit of a spoilsport. I imagine that boy may well have thought the same kind of thing about Philip Lawrence. But I am sure he doesn’t think that now. I imagine him thinking back over it all, and saying to himself something like ‘He gave his life for me – I would do anything to show him how thankful I am – if I could.’ But he can’t, because Philip Lawrence is dead.

In a lot of ways we are in the same sort of position as that lad. Jesus gave himself to save us. But one big difference is that Jesus is alive, so we can show him how grateful we are. Sometimes we get so used to hearing about what Jesus has done for us that it loses its impact. But when we understand what he has done and how much it cost him, how can we deliberately do anything that we know will hurt him or grieve him? If we remember what he has done for us then we will want to please him, we will want to devote ourselves to doing what is good.

rememberTheWholePictureWereHeadingForAWh.header: Remember the Whole Picture – We’re Heading for a Whole New Creation
rememberTheWholePictureWereHeadingForAWh.body:
Paul says that God saved us ‘so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs having the hope of eternal life’ (Titus 3:7). We are called to be co-heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). We have been adopted into a new family, we are children of God, brothers and sisters of Jesus and very soon we will be reigning with him in his New Creation for eternity (Revelation 22:5). Paul doesn’t go into great detail here, but this focus on eternity is a theme which runs right through the letter. Consider Titus 1:2, which speaks of ‘the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the beginning of time’. This promise, that a whole new world is coming, is the foundation on which our faith is built. Titus 2:13-14 makes the same sort of point: God’s grace teaches us how to live ‘while we wait for the blessed hope – the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good’.

The ultimate goal of Jesus’ rescue mission was to purify a people for his very own, completely free from sin, who will be with him for ever and who will worship him for ever in his New Creation. That is the ultimate goal. There are benefits to being a Christian now, but the best is still to come. The process of freeing us from the nightmare of sin that we looked at in verse 3 has begun, but it is not finished yet.

Titus 3:7 tells us that we have already been justified by God’s grace – God has taken the initiative to put us right with himself – which makes us heirs having the hope of eternal life. We are heirs, we have eternity in a whole new world to look forward to, even though we are not there yet. The reason that the New Creation is so good, is that we will be fully with God, and fully without sin. We will see God and Jesus face to face. And we ourselves will be the opposite of the description in Titus 3:3. Sometimes you can end up with the idea that holiness or godliness means being stuffy, boring, dull, and wishy-washy. But it is not like that at all. The New Creation will be tremendous because God will be there, and all the other people there will be godly. Instead of living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another, we will be living in kindness and peace, loving and caring for one another.

Just to begin to get a feel for the contrast between sin and hell, and godliness and the New Creation, let me pick out some of the key words Paul uses as he describes first our wretched situation in sin, and then God’s great rescue leading towards his New Creation. Titus 3:3 has the negative: ‘Foolish, disobedient, deceived, enslaved, malice, envy, hated, hating.’ And then Titus 3:4-7: ‘kindness, love, mercy, saved, rebirth, renewal, poured out, generously, justified, grace, heirs, hope, eternal life’. Real life means living a godly life, becoming more like Jesus, becoming more ready for that New Creation. Remember the whole picture – we are heading for a whole New Creation.

backToPeter.body:
At the start I asked what Peter should move on to next. Now you can see the answer: nothing else. He stays with the gospel.

So, those are three parts of the whole picture we have looked at: (i) Remember that sin destroys you; (ii) Remember the mercy you don’t deserve; and (iii) Remember that you are headed for the New Heavens and New Earth. Those are just summaries of three aspects of how the gospel motivates us to live a holy life, but they are exactly the sort of thing my friend Peter needs to hear to help him grow in his faith. And they are exactly the sort of thing we all need to hear, no matter how long we have been Christians. So whatever you do, don’t move on from the gospel, don’t grow out of the gospel, and don’t let something else take your eye off the gospel. If you lose sight of the gospel, you are losing sight of Jesus.

Titus 3:8 tells us that the gospel is ‘excellent and profitable for everyone’ and that we need to keep on trying to understand it better in all its implications. In this chapter we have been looking at how the gospel helps us devote ourselves to doing what is good – the same gospel applies to every aspect of the Christian life. The gospel makes us grow, the gospel leads to godliness.

keyPoints.body:
• The gospel does not only make us Christians. It also makes us grow (Titus 3:8).

  • Remember that sin destroys. It promises freedom, but it makes us slaves.

  • Remember the mercy we don’t deserve. We did not earn our way in, and we cannot earn our way to stay in.

  • Remember that a New Creation is coming, with God and without sin. That hope helps us live well now.

  • We never move on from the gospel. We come back to it again and again.

puttingItIntoPractice.body: Choose the one of these three reminders that you tend to forget: sin destroys; mercy I do not deserve; the New Creation. Write it on a card or in your phone. This week, when you are tempted to do something wrong, stop and say it to yourself, out loud if you can. At the end of the week, write down one time it helped. Then add this step to your Personal Gospel-Growth Plan from Chapter 1.

questionsForReflection.body:
• Before you read this chapter, what would you have said Peter should move on to next? Has your answer changed?

  • Titus 3:3 describes life without Christ. Which of those words do you still see in yourself at times?

  • Do you ever feel you must be good enough to stay in God’s good books? Where does that feeling come from?

  • When did you last think about the New Creation? How could that hope help you with something you face this week?

  • Which of the three reminders do you need today: sin destroys, mercy I do not deserve, or the New Creation?

footnotes.body: I owe three points in this chapter to Timothy Keller, Counterfeit Gods: When the Empty Promises of Love, Money and Power Let You Down (London: Hodder & Stoughton, 2009): that idols are usually good things made ultimate (Introduction); that Isaac became a risk to Abraham in this way (ch. 1); and that daydreams and strong emotions are clues to our idols (Epilogue). The ebook has no printed page numbers, so I cite by chapter.
Keller, Counterfeit Gods, Introduction.

By the way, this test of Abraham could only have worked at this point in salvation history, and at this point in progressive revelation. We have a lot more of God’s word than Abraham did. We know that God is the God of truth and order and coherence – not falsehood and confusion and chaos. We know that God never contradicts himself, and we know that God hates human sacrifice, because he has said so repeatedly (Leviticus 18:21, 20:2-5; Deuteronomy 18:10, 12:31; Psalm 106:37-41; Jeremiah 7:31; Ezekiel 16:20-21). But Abraham lived before these Scriptures were written. He may well have assumed that God hated human sacrifice, and he would have been right – but Genesis does not tell us what he knew, or on what basis. If Abraham had known for certain that God hated it, he would have been confused, and could have rightly replied to God, ‘But you have said you hate human sacrifice, and it is never to be done; and now you are saying you want it, and it should be done. I don’t understand!’ Of course, this situation would never arise, because God doesn’t contradict himself. Abraham’s test is not a pattern for us, because God has since made clear how much he hates human sacrifice – and so anyone claiming today that God is telling them to sacrifice someone is certainly wrong, because we know God hates human sacrifice, and God does not contradict himself.
Keller, Counterfeit Gods, ch. 1.

To be more precise, ‘sheep’ and ‘fish’ are words that look grammatically singular in English, yet in usage they serve for both the singular and the plural. ‘Elohim’ is the converse in Hebrew: it looks grammatically plural in Hebrew, yet in usage it serves for both the singular and the plural. The NIV footnote gives the other reading: ‘This is your god.’
Following standard convention, the NIV translates God’s name ‘Yahweh’ with small capitals into English: ‘the Lord’.

As 1 Kings 3:2 observes, a mitigating factor is that the Temple had not yet been built. The situation at Gibeon was also unusual: the tabernacle and its bronze altar were there (2 Chronicles 1:3-6), although the ark was in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 1:4). Deuteronomy 12:1-7 says that Israel should worship at the place the Lord chooses, and 1 Kings 3:3 says that Solomon showed his love for the Lord, except that he offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places.

introduction.body:
[[fn:1]]This chapter goes with Studies 12 and 13.

‘Dear children, keep yourselves from idols.’ (1 John 5:21)

Obinna sold phone accessories in a busy market. He started with one small table. Ten years later he had a shop with a roof, two workers and a sign with his name on it. He was a good man. He gave in church, and every Monday morning he prayed over the shop.

One night a fire went through the market. By morning the shop was gone.

Obinna lost his stock, and that was bad. But what frightened his wife was something else. He stopped eating. He stopped going to church. He said, ‘Without the shop, I am nobody.’

There is nothing wrong with a shop, or with working hard. A shop is a gift from God. But a gift can quietly take the place that belongs only to God. I have made up Obinna, so that no real person can be recognised. This chapter is about that quiet change. We will look at what an idol is, at three Bible stories, and at how to find the idols in our own hearts.

whatIsAnIdol.body:
There used to be a time when physical idols were common all over the world. In some places they still are common. I remember once going into a restaurant that was owned and run by a Hindu family. I was part-way through my meal, when I realised that some of the ‘decorations’ in one corner of the restaurant were not decorations at all. It was a small shrine, and it had some of the family’s images of their gods on it. If you come from one type of background, you may be used to seeing physical idols like that. If you come from another type of background, they may be very unfamiliar to you. But either way, when we hear the word ‘idol’ the picture that springs to mind is often a physical statue or image of some sort. The Bible certainly does use the word ‘idol’ that way – the second commandment states:

You shall not make for yourself an image in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters below. (Exodus 20:4)

That certainly includes statues and carvings and other physical representations and images. But the Bible’s understanding of idolatry goes further than that. Consider this verse from Paul:

Put to death, therefore, whatever belongs to your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, which is idolatry. (Colossians 3:5)

Greed is idolatry. You cannot see greed on a shelf, the way you can see a statue. It hides in the heart. How can greed be an idol? Paul explains it more in Romans:

For although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images made to look like a mortal human being and birds and animals and reptiles. Therefore God gave them over in the sinful desires of their hearts to sexual impurity for the degrading of their bodies with one another. They exchanged the truth about God for a lie, and worshipped and served created things rather than the Creator – who is for ever praised. Amen. (Romans 1:21-25)

The last sentence is key: ‘They exchanged the truth about God for a lie, and worshipped and served created things rather than the Creator.’ That gets to the core of what idolatry is – idolatry is when we worship or serve some created thing, instead of God the Creator. It is when we take something God has made, and we put it at the centre of our lives, instead of putting him there. Loving something deeply is not the problem. The problem comes when we ask it to give us what only God can give, or put it ahead of him. (And, as Paul points out, that normally goes along with exchanging some part of God’s truth for a falsehood.)

Tim Keller makes the point that idols often begin as good things.[[fn:2]] We take something good that God has made – a job, a marriage, a child, our health – and give it the place that belongs to God. It is then a god-thing. The things we turn into idols are part of God’s good creation, so they start out good. They become bad when we try to make them gods.

There is a classic example of that nearly happening in the story of Abraham.

wasIsaacAbrahamsIdol.body:
Think of the shape of Abraham’s life. At the age of 75 he leaves home and everything he knows, to live as a foreigner (Genesis 12:4). He does this because he trusts God, who has promised him blessing, land and descendants. Yet Abraham has no child. He waits another 25 years (Genesis 21:5).

Imagine for a moment that you are Abraham, and imagine you have been waiting all those decades for the child of promise to arrive – the one through whom blessing to the whole world will come. How would you feel when the child is actually born?

That is part of the point of the shocking story in Genesis 22. God suddenly asks Abraham to do the unthinkable:

Then God said, ‘Take your son, your only son, whom you love – Isaac – and go to the region of Moriah. Sacrifice him there as a burnt offering on a mountain that I will show you.’ (Genesis 22:2)

We know how the story ends, so it may not hit us as hard as it hit Abraham. God asks him to sacrifice Isaac – to kill him. How could God ask this?[[fn:3]] Genesis 22:1 tells us that God is testing him. Part of the answer, I think, is idolatry. Idols are good things that become god-things. For Abraham, Isaac is a gift he waited a lifetime for, and all his hopes are tied up in the boy. If you had asked Abraham, ‘What is everything to you?’ he might easily have said, ‘My son Isaac!’ But he should say, ‘God is everything to me! And Isaac is his gift.’

If we are not careful, good gifts become idols. In Genesis 22 God sets Abraham a stark choice between himself and Isaac.[[fn:4]] Abraham chooses God. That is what makes it safe for him to enjoy his son: Isaac is a gift again, and not a god.

This is, of course, not the last time idolatry raises its head for the people of God.

whyDidIsraelChooseAGoldenCalf.header: Why Did Israel Choose a Golden Calf?
whyDidIsraelChooseAGoldenCalf.body:
Exodus 32 tells a story of serious idolatry. God has just redeemed his people from slavery, overthrowing the superpower of the day (Egypt, via plagues), and defeating its army (in the Red Sea). Now they are brought to Mount Sinai, and God speaks to them in the thunder. They agree that Moses alone should go up the mountain to receive the Law, and they will wait below. So far so good. But then Moses is away a long time, and the people get bored and restless. This is not good, but it is perhaps understandable. But look at what they say:

When the people saw that Moses was so long in coming down from the mountain, they gathered round Aaron and said, ‘Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this fellow Moses who brought us up out of Egypt, we don’t know what has happened to him.’ (Exodus 32:1)

Aaron, for whatever reason, thinks it best to take control of this outburst of idol-making, and so he asks them for gold, which he fashions into the shape of a ‘calf’. This is probably not a ‘calf’ in the sense of a ‘baby bull’ but a ‘calf’ in the sense of a ‘young bull’ or a ‘youthful bull’. In other words they are not making an idol to represent infanthood, and weakness, and vulnerability, but rather an idol to represent youthfulness, and strength, and vigour. And this makes sense in the context of their deliverance from Egypt – defeating a superpower, ten plagues, parting the Red Sea – those are all acts of strength, and vigour, and power. That is why, when they see the idol, they say:

‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.’ (Exodus 32:4b)

They are probably thinking of divine strength and power, and focusing on those attributes. But why do they say ‘gods’ and not ‘god’? Well of course, they don’t say it in English at all. What they originally say is ‘Elohim’, which is the Hebrew word for ‘God’ – or it can mean ‘gods’. It’s a bit like the word ‘sheep’, or the word ‘fish’ in English: the singular and the plural are the same (so we say both ‘one sheep’ and ‘two sheep’ or ‘one fish’ and ‘two fish’).[[fn:5]] In this verse the Hebrew words for ‘these’ and for ‘brought up’ are both plural, so the NIV puts ‘gods’ in the main text. It puts the other option (‘god’) in the footnote.

Even so, Aaron may have meant the one God, as we can see from what he says:

When Aaron saw this, he built an altar in front of the calf and announced, ‘Tomorrow there will be a festival to the Lord.’ So the next day the people rose early and sacrificed burnt offerings and presented fellowship offerings. Afterwards they sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry. (Exodus 32:5-6)

Aaron still hopes to be able to salvage something from this idolatry. He thinks he can turn it into a festival to ‘the Lord’[[fn:6]] – a festival to Yahweh – with all the normal Old Testament practices like burnt offerings and fellowship offerings. Aaron is probably thinking something like this: ‘We can work with this: Yahweh is strong – he rescued us from Egypt. A calf-idol is strong – so it can represent Yahweh.’ But idol-worship is false worship. Look at God’s verdict on it:

Then the Lord said to Moses, ‘Go down, because your people, whom you brought up out of Egypt, have become corrupt. They have been quick to turn away from what I commanded them and have made themselves an idol cast in the shape of a calf. They have bowed down to it and sacrificed to it and have said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.”’ (Exodus 32:7-8)

God is appalled at their idolatry, even to the point where he is ready to disown them. If they turn away from him, and turn to their own man-made idols, then they are no longer living as his people. Just because Aaron calls it a ‘festival to Yahweh’ doesn’t mean it really is a festival to Yahweh. Words are important, but they can hide what we are actually doing. Aaron said this was a festival ‘to Yahweh’ – but it was not; it was idolatry.

We could say it even more sharply than that. Back in Chapter 2 we made the point that the lies that work are half-truths, or twisted truths. The same is true of idolatry. The idolatry that works is built on half-truths and twisted truths. That way someone can always point to the bits that are true, and correctly say, ‘This is true!’ – and at the same time distract us away from the falsehood. Worship can use the true God’s name and still be false worship, if it gives a false picture of him or ignores what he has commanded. Half-true worship of the true God is false worship of God, which is worship of a false god.

That is what is going on with Aaron and the Israelites here. ‘God is strong!’ they are saying. ‘God is mighty, he is powerful, he is virile! Our bull-calf expresses his strength and power. We serve the Almighty, and this representation helps us focus on that. It strengthens our worship of the Almighty God, the one whose arm is stronger than the might of Egypt.’ All – or most – of this is true. But just because there are true bits, that does not make it right. The true bits are not the problem. It is the false or twisted bits that sit alongside the true bits. It is the missing bits of truth that have been left out and suppressed. It is precisely because you can point out the true bits, that half-truths are so dangerous. Of course half-truths have true bits – otherwise they wouldn’t be half-truths!

Which leads us on to one particular example of the danger of half-truths.

howBlessingsCanHoldYouBack.header: How Blessings Can Hold You Back
howBlessingsCanHoldYouBack.body:
We generally think of blessings as a good thing – of course we do! They are good things! That is certainly true. But we have seen that it is not enough for something to be true – half-truths are true, as far as they go. But by definition they are not the whole truth. The Bible does give us the whole truth – if we pay attention to all of it. Solomon’s story shows us clearly one of the sneaky things about the sin of idolatry, namely the way it turns good things into god-things – and therefore into bad things. That’s the irony – it transforms good things into things that are bad for us.

The Bible shows us this transformation in detail in the life of Solomon. His story starts off very well. In 1 Kings 3, he is sacrificing to the Lord at one of the ‘High Places’, at Gibeon, which was not ideal.[[fn:7]] But God graciously overlooks this, and appears to him, and asks him to choose a blessing: ‘Ask for whatever you want me to give you’ (1 Kings 3:5b). Solomon wisely chooses to receive (more) wisdom, and God, who is pleased with this choice, grants him not only the asked-for wisdom, but several other blessings as well:

‘Since you have asked for this and not for long life or wealth for yourself, nor have asked for the death of your enemies but for discernment in administering justice, I will do what you have asked. I will give you a wise and discerning heart, so that there will never have been anyone like you, nor will there ever be. Moreover, I will give you what you have not asked for – both wealth and honour – so that in your lifetime you will have no equal among kings. And if you walk in obedience to me and keep my decrees and commands as David your father did, I will give you a long life.’ (1 Kings 3:11-14)

And a few chapters later the blessings come to fulfilment. Solomon has ruled wisely, he has peace on every side, he has amassed great wealth, and his fame has spread far and wide – so much so that the Queen of Sheba sets out on a trip to see Solomon’s court for herself. And she is impressed:

The report I heard in my own country about your achievements and your wisdom is true. But I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes. Indeed, not even half was told me; in wisdom and wealth you have far exceeded the report I heard. How happy your people must be! How happy your officials, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Praise be to the Lord your God, who has delighted in you and placed you on the throne of Israel. Because of the Lord’s eternal love for Israel, he has made you king to maintain justice and righteousness. (1 Kings 10:6-9)

The picture we are given of Solomon’s court is bright and beautiful and glorious and good. And yet, we know that it all so quickly falls apart. In the very next chapter he takes hundreds of foreign wives and concubines, and builds pagan temples for them, and is led astray into worshipping their gods, so that:

The Lord became angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice. Although he had forbidden Solomon to follow other gods, Solomon did not keep the Lord’s command. (1 Kings 11:9-10)

How did it all fall apart so quickly? It turns out the cracks were there, if you knew where to look for them, even while things seemed to be going so well. Consider these verses from Deuteronomy, that set out how the kings of Israel are to conduct themselves:

The king … must not acquire great numbers of horses for himself or make the people return to Egypt to get more of them, for the Lord has told you, ‘You are not to go back that way again.’ He must not take many wives, or his heart will be led astray. He must not accumulate large amounts of silver and gold. (Deuteronomy 17:16-17)

There are four requirements for the king to observe:

  • No stock-piling of horses. (Horses were a military asset in those days.)

  • No returning to Egypt to get the horses.

  • No accumulating of gold and silver.

  • No taking of many wives.

How does Solomon do on these four counts? Not well – not well at all. Even in 1 Kings 10, where things are going so well, they are at the same time going very badly. Let’s consider the requirements one by one:

  • No stock-piling of horses.
    Solomon fails on this one, and on a massive scale: ‘Solomon accumulated chariots and horses; he had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses, which he kept in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem’ (1 Kings 10:26). By anybody’s measure, 12,000 is a lot of horses.

  • No returning to Egypt to get the horses.
    Solomon also fails on the second requirement: ‘Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue – the royal merchants purchased them from Kue at the current price. They imported a chariot from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty. They also exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and of the Arameans’ (1 Kings 10:28-29). It turns out Egypt is one of the two key places that Solomon sends his people to, to buy horses. Not only that, he has become the main local horse-and-chariot businessman – the regional arms-dealer, in other words.

  • No accumulating of gold and silver.
    Solomon also breaks the third requirement, and does so spectacularly: ‘The weight of the gold that Solomon received yearly was 666 talents [about 23 tonnes!], not including the revenues from merchants and traders and from all the Arabian kings and the governors of the territories. … King Solomon was greater in riches and wisdom than all the other kings of the earth. … The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore-fig trees in the foothills’ (1 Kings 10:14-15, 23, 27). Solomon is overflowing with gold, and as for silver – well, it becomes just a common, everyday thing.

  • No taking of many wives.
    It is well-known how this regulation is broken: ‘King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women … He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines, and his wives led him astray. As Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not fully devoted to the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father had been. He followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and Molek the detestable god of the Ammonites. So Solomon did evil in the eyes of the Lord; he did not follow the Lord completely, as David his father had done’ (1 Kings 11:1, 3-6).

The tragedy of Solomon is that despite all the blessing he receives, he goes astray. The irony of Solomon is that the very blessings themselves seem to play a role in leading him astray – or rather, sin twists the blessings into idols. Solomon delights in wealth, power, and status so much that he puts these things ahead of God, and ahead of obedience to God.

What he should have done is this: Solomon should have received his blessings from God, and used them in service to God, even when that meant putting God ahead of the blessings. (If he had done this he might have ended up less wealthy, but more faithful; he might have chosen fewer wives and more obedience.) What he actually did was that he put the blessings ahead of the Blesser – and disaster resulted.

whatAboutYou.body:
Here are some questions to find out whether you have made idols, or are in danger of making new ones. Do not be surprised if you find some. Our hearts keep making idols, so unless we keep repenting, they build up.

Think about your hopes. When nothing else needs your mind, where do your thoughts go? What do you picture when you daydream? Is there something you think would change your whole life, if only you could have it? ‘If only I were rich, everything would be all right.’ ‘If only I were married …’ Hoping is not wrong, and these things are good gifts. The problem begins when we stop seeing them as gifts from the Saviour, and start treating them as our salvation.

Think about your fears. What would feel like the end of your world, if it happened? Fear shows us where we look for security. Idols are only created things, and created things can be lost. If you lose something good, you will grieve, and that is right. Grief can make life feel empty for a time, and that does not mean you made an idol of what you lost. But if you find, over a long time, that you cannot see any hope without that thing, it is worth asking whether it had become more than a gift.

If you are grieving now, please hear this: grief is not idolatry, and this chapter is not an accusation. Grieve, and talk to someone you trust. If grief ever leaves you thinking of ending your life, tell a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor today.

Look at your time and your money, and ask whom you want to please, and where you run for comfort. They also show what we trust.

Which of God’s gifts could you be turning into an idol? Family, health, wealth, success, status, skills, popularity, influence, acceptance … Is one of these taking God’s place?

God can use hard times to show us where our trust has gone wrong. But we cannot assume that a particular loss happened for that reason, and a loss is never proof that you did something wrong. If you are turning a blessing into an idol, you have three paths:

  • You repent. You turn from the idol and refocus on God – even if that means holding it more loosely for a time. In time, you may be able to enjoy it as a blessing and not as an idol.

  • You carry on worshipping it. It keeps its hold on you, and you may pay a high price, until you see it, repent and turn back to him.

  • You carry on worshipping it, and God lets you. It pulls you further from him, and the damage can be deep.

What will you choose? The wise choice is the first path. No one else can choose it for you. You would be wise to start today.

turningToJesus.body:
Finding an idol is not the end. If we only take something away, we leave an empty place, and an empty place soon fills again. Paul says that the Thessalonians ‘turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God’ (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Notice the two movements: they turned from idols, and they turned to God. That is repentance and faith, which are for the whole of the Christian life, and not only for the day we first believe.

Idols cannot keep their promises. When they fall, they fall with us. Jesus is different. Satan once offered him all the kingdoms of the world, with their wealth and power – everything an idol promises. Jesus answered, ‘Worship the Lord your God, and serve him only’ (Matthew 4:10). He then went to the cross for us. Because of him we can come to God with our idols, and with our fear of losing them. He does not wait until we have cleared our hearts. He forgives us when we turn. He can be trusted with everything we are afraid to lose – even when we lose it, and do not understand why.

So when you find an idol, do not only say, ‘I must stop.’ Tell God what you have found. Tell him you have been trusting it, and ask him to forgive you. Then ask him to be what you were looking for.

backToObinna.body: Obinna’s pastor sat with him for weeks, and nobody told him his grief was wrong. His grief did not disappear at once. Slowly Obinna saw that he had been letting the shop tell him who he was. He told God so, and asked his forgiveness. Later he rebuilt, smaller. ‘The shop is still a good gift,’ he says. ‘But it is not my life.’

keyPoints.body:
• An idol is anything we put at the centre of our lives in place of God.

  • Idols often begin as good gifts. They become idols when we ask them to give what only God can.

  • Half-true worship of the true God is still false worship.

  • Our hopes and our fears show us our idols.

  • We deal with idols by turning from them and to Jesus, again and again.

puttingItIntoPractice.body:
Answer these seven questions. Do not answer ‘God’. Name a created thing.[[fn:8]]

  • What do I feel I must have to be happy?

  • What do I fear losing, or never gaining?

  • What made me bitter, and what can I not forgive?

  • Where do my time and money go?

  • What am I willing to lie for?

  • Where do I turn for comfort?

  • Whose approval do I want?

If question 3 brings up a deep hurt, Chapter 10 may help. Finding it hard to forgive is not the same as refusing to.

Choose one idol. This week, tell God what you have found, and ask him to forgive you and help you turn to him. Then choose one small action that shows you are putting God first, such as turning down a dishonest gain, or spending in prayer the time you would have given to the idol. And tell one trusted person, as Chapter 13 describes. Study 13 has the full quiz.

questionsForReflection.body:
• Think of a good gift God has given you. What would it mean to hold it with open hands?

  • When you daydream, what do you picture? What does that tell you?

  • Aaron called the festival ‘to the Lord’. Is there anything in your life that you call by God’s name but that is really about something else?

  • Think of a time when a loss felt too big. What had that thing meant to you?

  • What would it look like this week to turn from one idol, and to Jesus?
