introduction.body:
[[fn:1]]This chapter goes with Study 14.

‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.’ (Proverbs 1:7)

Picture two young men who finish university in the same year. Both are clever. Both want to do well.

One day a friend tells them about an investment scheme. ‘Give us ₦200,000 now,’ he says, ‘and we will pay you double in one month.’ Everyone is talking about it. A few people say they have already been paid.

The first man thinks, ‘I am a graduate. I can see a good deal.’ He borrows the money and pays in.

The second man is just as clever. But he has a habit. Before he decides anything big, he prays. He asks what the Bible says about honest gain. And he talks to an older believer he trusts. This older believer asks him two plain questions: ‘Who is paying the first people? Where does the money come from?’ The young man keeps his money.

I have made up these two men, and the other people in this chapter. But you may have seen something like it. The difference between them is not brains. It is wisdom.

Knowledge is knowing facts. Wisdom is knowing what to do with them, in a real situation, today. This chapter asks how we grow in it.

whatWisdomIs.body:
Wisdom is the skill of living in God’s way, in God’s world. It touches money, work, marriage, friendships, what we watch and what we say.

The Bible says wisdom starts with God. ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge’ (Proverbs 1:7). ‘Fear’ here does not mean being terrified. It means deep respect and wonder. It means taking God seriously: knowing who he is, trusting him, and honouring him as the one who made us and knows how life works. A child who loves her father is not afraid of him the way she would fear a robber. But she takes his words seriously. Proverbs 9:10 says it again, and adds that knowing the Holy One is what brings understanding.

This matters because God’s thoughts are not our thoughts. He says his ways are as far above ours as the heavens are above the earth (Isaiah 55:8-9). We cannot close that gap by being clever. We need God to come to us, and he has. Paul says that Christ Jesus has become for us ‘wisdom from God’ (1 Corinthians 1:30).

That is good news, and it changes how we read the rest of this chapter. We do not earn wisdom by good habits. We are given Christ, and then we learn to live as people who belong to him. I want to suggest four habits. They are not steps we climb to reach God. They are ways of staying close to the one who already holds us, like a farmer who tends the field that is already his.[[fn:2]]

Two of the habits are about taking wisdom in: the Bible and prayer. One is about sharing life with others. One is about turning away from what harms us. Wisdom grows slowly. No one becomes wise in a week. But it does grow.

listenLetTheBibleShapeHowYouThink.header: Listen: Let the Bible Shape How You Think
listenLetTheBibleShapeHowYouThink.body:
Think about how akara is made. (Akara are bean cakes, fried in oil and sold at roadsides across Nigeria.) Before the cook can make them, she soaks the beans in water. If she skips this, she cannot take off the skins, and the cakes do not come out right. The soaking changes the beans.

The word ‘steep’ means that kind of soaking. Horatius Bonar, a Scottish pastor of the nineteenth century, put it like this: ‘He that would be holy must steep himself in the Word, must bask in the sunshine which radiates from each page of revelation.’[[fn:3]] Here, ‘the Word’ means God’s written word – the Bible. ‘Holy’ means set apart for God and becoming like Jesus. Bonar’s picture is of a person who does not just visit the Bible but stays in it, as the beans stay in the water, or as a person stays in the sun on a cool harmattan morning, in the dry, dusty season.

Why the Bible? Because it tells us what God is like and how life works. Jesus prayed that his Father would make his people holy by the truth, and he said the Father’s word is truth (John 17:17). When we read the Bible, we are not just collecting information. God’s Spirit uses his word to change what we love, what we fear and what we choose.

The Bible also helps us test what we hear. Much is said in God’s name, and some of it is true and some is not. The believers in Berea listened to Paul eagerly, and then they checked what he said against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). We should do the same with every preacher, book and video – including this book.

Here is what this can look like. Imagine a market trader, Grace, who sells cloth. Before she opens her stall each morning, she reads a few verses and thinks about them while she arranges her goods. One Saturday a customer offers her a good price if she will sell cheap cloth as the expensive kind. ‘Nobody will know,’ he says. Grace has no time to look anything up. But the verses are still in her mind: God made her, God sees her, and God cares how she does business. She says no, politely. She loses the sale. But she keeps her good name in the market, and she sleeps well that night.

Try this. Choose a short passage. A few verses of Proverbs is a good place to start. Read it slowly, twice. Then ask three questions:

  • What does this show me about God?

  • What does it show me about myself?

  • What will I do about it today?

If reading is slow for you, or English is not your first language, you can listen to the Bible on audio, or read it with a friend. What matters is that the words go in. And go to preaching and Bible study too. We need to hear God’s word explained, not only read it alone.

askPrayForWisdom.body:
Most of us have met the driver who is lost but will not wind down his window to ask for directions. He drives round for an hour, and wastes petrol and patience, because asking feels like admitting something.

We can be like that with God. James writes, ‘If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God,’ and he adds that God gives generously and does not scold us for asking (James 1:5). Notice the invitation. We do not lack wisdom because God is stingy. We often lack it because we have not asked.

Prayer is also where wisdom and sin meet. J. C. Ryle, an English bishop of the nineteenth century, wrote: ‘Praying and sinning will never live together in the same heart. Prayer will consume sin, or sin will choke prayer.’[[fn:4]] To ‘consume’ is to burn up, as fire burns up dry grass. To ‘choke’ is what weeds do to a young plant. Ryle’s point is that we cannot keep both. When we pray honestly, sin loses ground. When we cling to a sin, prayer can become hard.

I want to be careful here. This is not a test to see how you are doing. If prayer has felt dry for a long time, that is not a verdict on you. It is a sign to come back to your Father, who is not counting your minutes. A short, honest prayer is real prayer.

Here is what one sentence of prayer can do. Imagine a mother, Hauwa, whose teenage son comes home late again. She is tired and angry, and the words are ready in her mouth. As she stands at the door, she prays silently, ‘Lord, give me wisdom.’ It takes three seconds. Then she says, ‘Are you all right?’ before she says, ‘Where have you been?’ Her son still has to answer for being late. But the conversation begins with care, not a shouting match, and he is more ready to listen.

Try this. Before you sign, send, say yes or reply in anger, stop for a few seconds and pray one sentence: ‘Lord, give me wisdom.’ It takes no time, and it turns a habit of reacting into a habit of asking. Also, when you finish reading the Bible each day, turn what you read into a prayer. If the passage showed you something about God, thank him for it. If it showed you something about yourself, ask him to change it.

walkWithOthers.body:
If you have ever cooked on firewood, you know that one stick left by itself will not burn for long. Put several sticks together and the fire holds. Take one away and it fades.

Wisdom works like that. The writer to the Hebrews tells us not to give up meeting together, but to encourage one another (Hebrews 10:24-25). Proverbs says, ‘As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another’ (Proverbs 27:17), and it says that if we walk with the wise, we become wise (Proverbs 13:20). Paul gives the other side: bad company ruins good habits (1 Corinthians 15:33). The people around us shape us, whether we plan it or not.

An Akan proverb says, ‘Wisdom is like a baobab tree; no one individual can embrace it.’[[fn:5]] A baobab trunk is so wide that one person’s arms will not go round it. In the same way, no one person has all the wisdom they need. We need other people’s eyes, experience and correction.

God’s plan is that we grow together. Paul describes the church as a body where every part has work to do, so that the whole body grows up (Ephesians 4:11-16). Change is not a solo journey. It is, in Tim Chester’s phrase, ‘a community project’.[[fn:6]] Your local church is where God means you to learn wisdom, because it is where you will meet people of different ages, who have walked with Jesus for many years.

Not every group is a good one, so it helps to ask four questions about the fellowship you belong to:

  • Does it put Christ first?

  • Does it teach the Bible and test things by it?

  • Does it deal honestly with sin, suffering and people who are hurting?

  • Does it help people follow Christ, tell the truth and care for one another – or does it use fear, money or control?

No church is perfect, and I am not asking you to look for one. I am asking you to look for one that is going in the right direction.

Here is what a wisdom friend can do. Imagine a young engineer, Chinedu, who is offered a contract that looks very good. He is excited and ready to sign. But he takes it first to Mr Bello, an older man in his church who has run a business for years. Mr Bello reads it slowly and finds a clause that would leave Chinedu paying for the other company’s mistakes. Chinedu had not noticed it. He was not careless. He simply needed another pair of eyes, and he was wise enough to ask for them.

Try this. Ask one wise believer, someone further on in the journey than you, to be your ‘wisdom friend’. Bring them one real decision you are facing and ask what they see. Then listen. We will return to friendship and accountability in Chapter 13.

runFromWhatHarmsYou.body:
Wisdom is not only knowing what to do. It is also knowing what to stay away from. The book of Proverbs says: do not set foot on the path of the wicked; avoid it, do not travel on it, turn from it and go on your way (Proverbs 4:14-15).

A driver who knows that a road floods in the rainy season does not ask, ‘How close can I get to the flood?’ He takes another road. Yet when it comes to sin, many of us ask exactly that question. ‘How far can I go?’ ‘Is it really a sin if I only do this?’ Tim Chester suggests a different question: ‘Don’t ask, “How far can I go toward sin?” Ask instead, “How far can I run from sin?”’[[fn:7]] That is how Paul spoke. He told Timothy to flee the evil desires of youth (2 Timothy 2:22) and told the Corinthians to flee from idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14).

Running starts with knowing where you fall. Many of us fall in the same way again and again: the same place, the same company, the same time of night, the same mood. Write them down. Then plan a different road. God promises that when we are tempted, he will provide a way out (1 Corinthians 10:13). Wisdom often means taking that way out early – leaving the room, switching off the phone, going home, calling a friend.

Here is how it works in practice. Imagine a young man, Tunde, who struggles with betting on football. Betting apps are easy to find on a phone, and the matches come every weekend. Tunde noticed that his trouble did not begin on Saturday. It began on Friday night, when he opened the app ‘just to look at the odds’. By Saturday afternoon he had placed bets he could not afford. So he stopped asking, ‘Can I bet a little?’ He asked, ‘Where does this start?’ Then he took a different road. He deleted the apps on Friday afternoon, before the temptation came, and he asked his younger brother to ask him on Sunday how the weekend went.

If a habit is stronger than you are, talk to your pastor, a wise Christian, or a doctor or counsellor you trust. That is not weakness. It is wisdom.

And do not hide it. Sin grows in secret. James tells believers to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16). So tell a mature, trustworthy believer where you struggle. That is why the habits belong together: the friend helps you run, prayer gives you strength, and the Bible shows you what is worth running towards. Chapter 13 says more about whom to tell and how.

If you fall, do not run from God. Run to him. His grace is not only what saves us; it also teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives (Titus 2:11-12). We will look at how to come back after a fall in Chapter 11.

backToTheTwoMen.body: Go back to the two young men at the start. The second man did not keep his money because he knew more. He kept it because of what he did. He took God seriously. He asked God for wisdom. He listened to someone older. He kept away from a path that looked too good to be true. These are habits, and they are open to every reader of this chapter – the new believer as much as the church leader. You can begin today.

keyPoints.body:
• Wisdom is knowing how to live in God’s way, and it begins with knowing and honouring God.

  • Christ is our wisdom. The four habits are ways of staying close to him, not ways of earning his favour.

  • Stay in the Bible, and test everything you hear by it.

  • Ask God for wisdom often and simply. Keep bringing your sin to God in prayer; do not make peace with it.

  • Walk with wise people, and run from the things that harm you.

puttingItIntoPractice.body:
This week, make a four-line wisdom plan. Write it on a card or in your phone.

  • Listen. When and where will I read the Bible each day, and which passage will I start with?

  • Ask. What decision am I facing, and when will I pray for wisdom about it?

  • Walk. Who is one wise believer I will talk to this week?

  • Run. What is the one place, person or habit I need to stay away from?

Show the plan to the believer you named in line 3. Look at it again in a week, and again in a month. If you made the Personal Gospel-Growth Plan in Chapter 1, keep the two together.

Use it with Study 14. If you are going through Study 14 in the Personal Workbook, you have already met some of these ideas. The study asks what resources, people and practices help you grow in wisdom. Your four-line plan is a way to answer that question with names, times and places. You may also have taken the Wisdom Check-up. Statements 9 and 10 (about your instincts and thinking being shaped by Bible principles) point to the first habit, ‘Listen’. Statement 1 (about learning life lessons from others) points to the third, ‘Walk’. Bring your plan to your group, and ask one person to check in with you after a week.

questionsForReflection.body:
• Think of the last big decision you made. Did you pray, read the Bible and ask someone wise? What happened?

  • Which of the four habits is strongest in your life now? Which is weakest? What gets in the way?

  • Who are the people closest to you? Do they draw you towards wisdom or away from it?

  • Where do you tend to fall? What would it look like to take a different road?

  • What difference does it make that Christ himself is your wisdom, and not your habits?

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Grow in Christ
intro: These notes are designed to help group leaders and mentors get the most out of each chapter – both for the people they are leading and for themselves. They are not a substitute for working through the material yourself first. The best leaders are those who have worked through the questions personally before they help others doing the same.

Create a safe space for honesty. The questions in this study are designed to prompt real reflection, not just correct answers. Your job is to make the group feel safe enough to say what they actually think, not what they think a Christian is supposed to say.
Don’t rush the silences. Some of the best moments in a group study happen after a question lands and nobody speaks for a few seconds. Resist the urge to fill every silence.
Watch for the person who goes quiet. Sometimes the most significant thing happening in the room is with the person who says the least. Check in with them afterwards.

keyPoints.body:
This session introduces shame and how it differs from guilt: guilt says ‘I did something wrong’; shame says ‘I am wrong’. Luka’s story gives the problem a human face, and ‘What would you tell Luka?’ deserves plenty of time.

Genesis 2:25 and 3:1–13 show shame entering the world, and three ways Adam and Eve respond: covering up, hiding and blaming. The prodigal son shows what God does about shame: the father runs, embraces and restores.

The older brother shows that shame can also work through pride and anger. Matthew 5:38–48 shows Jesus’ way of breaking the cycle of retaliation and honour.

pastorals.body:
Luka’s struggle with pornography will be real for some in the group, and many will carry other secrets. Do not ask anyone to disclose anything in the session, and make clear that what is said in the group is not to be repeated outside it.

Not all shame comes from our own sin. If someone has been abused or wronged, the shame they feel is not theirs to carry and is not something to confess. Do not press the reflection questions on someone for whom they cut too close, and be ready to point them to a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor.

The second reflection question asks about being too ashamed to ask for help. Someone may answer it by being honest in the room for the first time. Receive them as the father received his son.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who take Luka’s story as being about someone else, and for those who deal with shame by shaming others. The father and the older brother are both in the story for a reason.

keyPoints.body:
Study 8 looked at shame. This session turns to God’s answer. God delights in his children (Zephaniah 3:17), and our honour comes from him and not from our performance. The five verses are for slow meditation, not quick answers.

The way out of shame is confession, to God and to one another (Psalm 32, James 5:16, Galatians 6:2). The world’s code says to cover up; God’s way is to bring it into the open and be forgiven.

Daniel 12:2 reminds us that God’s verdict is the one that lasts, so whose approval we live for matters.

pastorals.body:
The Guilt and Shame Experience Scale is a research tool, adapted here as a way into conversation. It is not a diagnosis and has no score or cut-off. Please do not ask anyone to share their answers. If someone is clearly distressed, encourage them to talk to a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor.

Confession needs a safe person. The book advises choosing one mature, trustworthy person who will treat you with dignity and keep what you say private unless someone is in danger. Help the group think about what makes someone safe before anyone confesses anything, and do not press people to say more than they choose.

The chapter says more about choosing whom to tell, including guidance for those who are attracted to people of their own sex. Read it before the session.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who give the ‘right’ answer, that God’s honour matters more, while living as if the world’s honour matters more. The first reflection question asks about practice as well as principle.

keyPoints.body:
This session starts from a question: once someone understands the gospel, what do they need next? Titus 3 answers: the same gospel. It saves us, and it makes us grow.

The first of three ways the gospel makes us grow is to remember that sin destroys. Proverbs, Romans, Galatians, 1 Corinthians, Isaiah and James each show a different side: sin traps and enslaves, it fights against the Spirit, it harms us and our relationship with God, and it ends in death. The picture of drug addiction in the chapter helps here.

The aim is not fear for its own sake, but a bigger motive for doing good.

pastorals.body:
Some in the group may be caught in a sin that has enslaved them, and the language of slavery, death and hell may land hard. Keep returning to the gospel: the point of seeing sin’s power is to run to Christ, not to despair.

The last reflection question asks people to imagine embracing a sin they are tempted by. Make clear that this is a way of seeing where sin ends, and not an invitation to dwell on it.

Do not let the group treat Peter as someone else’s case study. His story is everyone’s.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for the idea that growth means moving on from the gospel to ‘deeper’ things. Paul tells Titus to keep insisting on the basics.

keyPoints.body:
The second and third ways the gospel makes us grow are to remember the mercy we do not deserve and to remember the whole New Creation. Mercy is the heart of the gospel: God saved us on the basis of his mercy and not our works (Titus 3:5), and his mercy is renewed every morning.

Titus 1:1 links truth and godliness: understanding the gospel changes us. The chapter says carefully that this is not a test to frighten anyone, and that growth is uneven.

The New Creation passages (Revelation 21–22) give a hope that motivates holiness now.

pastorals.body:
The last two reflection questions are about assurance. Some people are very sure and some are not. Some feel sure for the wrong reasons, and some feel unsure even though they trust Christ. The aim is that each person’s answer rests on what Christ has done and not on how well they have done.

The Gospel Check-up is not a test and has no score. Please do not compare answers in the group. Anyone anxious about whether they are saved should be encouraged to talk to a pastor.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who think they must be good enough to stay in God’s good books. The study names that lie and answers it with Titus 3:5.

keyPoints.body:
This session widens the idea of an idol from statues to anything we put at the centre of life in place of God: greed, desires, even good gifts. Luther’s quotation sets the theme.

Isaac shows how a good gift can become a ‘god-thing’, and how God tests whether the Giver comes first. The golden calf shows how easily idolatry can be dressed up as worship of the Lord, and that half-true worship is false worship.

The last verses call us to guard ourselves against idols and to flee from them.

pastorals.body:
Idolatry can feel remote for some groups and very close for others. Where physical idols are part of the group’s world, be respectful but clear that the Bible’s concern goes beyond statues to the heart.

Abraham’s test is shocking. The chapter notes that it could only have happened at that point in the story and is not a pattern for us. God hates human sacrifice, and no one today should think God is asking them to sacrifice someone.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who name only ‘safe’ idols, such as money or phones, and skip good gifts such as family, ministry or reputation.

keyPoints.body:
Solomon shows how blessings can hold us back. His story begins with a good request and a generous God, and ends with a heart turned to other gods. The cracks were there early: Deuteronomy 17:16–17 named four dangers, and Solomon broke all four while things looked glorious.

The Idolatry Detection Quiz uses seven questions to uncover what we rely on. The three paths at the end give a choice: repent; carry on and pay a price; or carry on and be left to it. The wise choice is to repent, and to start today.

pastorals.body:
The quiz asks personal questions. Please do not ask anyone to share their answers; invite people to say whatever they choose. Question 3 (what made me most bitter) may bring up a deep hurt, including abuse. Finding it hard to forgive is not the same as refusing to, so help people to find proper support from a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor.

Fear and loss are part of this session. Grief is not idolatry, and a loss is never proof that someone did something wrong. If anyone mentions thoughts of ending their life, take it seriously, stay with them, and help them speak to a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor that day.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who hear the session as an accusation. Blessings are good gifts, and the point is to hold them with open hands.

keyPoints.body:
Wisdom is applying knowledge to life, at the right time and in the right way, and it begins with knowing and fearing God. Proverbs 26:4–5 shows that we need wisdom even to use wisdom: wisdom is like a ladder.

Christ is our wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:30), so growing in wisdom means growing close to him. The chapter gives four habits for gaining it: listen, ask, walk and run. Stay in God’s word, ask him for wisdom, walk with wise people, and run from what harms us.

pastorals.body:
The Wisdom Check-up is not a test and has no score. People who feel unwise may find it discouraging. Remind them that James 1:5 promises wisdom to those who ask, and that God gives without scolding.

The reflection about a recent foolish situation may bring up a painful memory. Let people choose how much to say.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who think wisdom is the same as being clever or well read. The study’s point is that wisdom starts with knowing God.

blocks.title: Christians who want to grow
blocks.body: If you are already a Christian but feel like your growth has stalled — or if you simply want to grow more — this study is for you. It works through what the Bible says about growing in Jesus: what holds us back, how grace works, and how to get moving again. The goal is not guilt, but growth.

blocks.title: New Christians
blocks.body: If you have recently come to faith, this study will help you build on the foundations. It looks at how God deals with shame, why the gospel is for the whole Christian life, the danger of idols, and how to grow in wisdom. Working through it carefully will give you something solid to build on.

blocks.title: People exploring Christianity
blocks.body: If you are not yet a Christian but are genuinely curious — wondering what the Christian life actually involves, what it demands, and what it offers — this study is for you too. It doesn’t assume you’ve already made up your mind. It works through what the Bible says and invites you to think carefully about it.

blocks.title: People discipling others
blocks.body: If you are walking alongside someone else in their faith — as a mentor, a small group leader, or a friend — this study gives you a structured way to work through the essentials of spiritual growth together. The seven sessions in this volume cover shame, the gospel, idols and wisdom.

blocks.title: Studies 8–14
blocks.body: This is volume 2 of Grow in Christ. Volume 1 covers Studies 1–7, and volume 2 continues with Studies 8–14. You can use volume 2 on its own, but it helps to have worked through volume 1 first.

blocks.title: The companion book
blocks.body:
At the end of Studies 9, 11, 13 and 14 you will find a Read more button. It takes you to the matching chapter of the companion book, which you will also find under The book in the contents menu.

Do each study first, then read the chapter. Chapters 4–7 are in this volume; the book has 14 chapters in all.

blocks.title: On your own
blocks.body: This study works well as a personal study. Work through each chapter at your own pace, read the Bible passages, write your answers to the questions, and meditate on the reflection questions at the end. There is no right speed — some chapters may take twenty minutes, others may take longer if a question stops you in your tracks.

blocks.title: In a group
blocks.body: The study also works well in a small group setting. You could work through each chapter together from scratch, reading the passages and discussing the questions as a group. Alternatively — and this is often the most rewarding approach — each person works through the chapter individually first, writes their answers, and then the group comes together to discuss what they found. Either way works. The questions are designed to prompt genuine reflection, not just right answers.

blocks.title: Working with a leader or mentor
blocks.body:
It can make a real difference to have someone guiding you through the study — a group leader, a pastor, or a more experienced Christian who can help you think through your answers and questions. Perhaps they are the one who recommended this study to you in the first place.

At the end of each chapter, the Share button lets you send your written answers directly to your leader or mentor — via WhatsApp, email, or any other app on your phone. This gives them a window into your thinking before you meet, and makes for much richer conversation.

blocks.title: Two kinds of questions
blocks.body: Each chapter has two kinds of questions. The Bible questions are tied to specific passages — asking you to look carefully at what the text says. The reflection questions at the end are more personal — asking what the chapter means for you specifically.

blocks.title: Key idea boxes
blocks.body: In Study 8 you will meet a darker-coloured card headed Key idea. It explains an idea, here the difference between guilt and shame, that is often misunderstood. Take a moment to think about what you understand by it, then tap the card to see a short clarification.

paras: Rick Creighton grew up in Northern Ireland and studied maths at Oxford and then taught maths at a secondary school in England. After that, he studied theology at Moore Theological College in Sydney and London School of Theology.

He served as a church pastor in England for ten years, before moving to Nigeria in 2012, where he has been teaching at ECWA Theological Seminary Kagoro and Jos ECWA Theological Seminary. He has been involved with BeaconLight Training since 2003.
Rick is married to Alanna. They have three children: Asha, Conor, and Jack.

paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
